add.issue.name: URGENT: the SSU2 session's received-packet set grows without bound and is scanned linearly

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## Question

None — this is a defect, and it is the most severe one on the board. Every SSU2 session eventually stops carrying traffic, and nothing about the failure says why.

`i2p_ssu2_conn` keeps a `seen_in` list of received packet numbers so a retransmit is not processed twice. It is prepended to on every new packet and **never pruned**. It is initialised to empty during the handshake and after that the only other writes are a prepend in the data path and a prepend of packet zero. Nothing removes an entry, for the life of the session.

The membership test that reads it is a linear `lists:member/2`, so the cost per inbound datagram grows with the number of datagrams the session has ever received. This is quadratic over a session's life and unbounded in memory.

## Measured

Cost of the membership test on a **new** packet number (the common case, and the one that must traverse the whole list):

| packets seen | µs per datagram | session heap |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.17 | 1.6 KB |
| 1,000 | 1.41 | 16 KB |
| 10,000 | 23.1 | 156 KB |
| 100,000 | 223 | 1.5 MB |
| 1,000,000 | 1,599 | 15.6 MB |

16 bytes of heap per entry, since each entry is a cons cell holding a boxed integer.

On a busy transit session at ~1,000 packets/second: 10 seconds of traffic is 23 µs per datagram, 100 seconds is 223 µs, and one hour is roughly 3.6 million entries at about 3.6 ms of scan per datagram and 56 MB of heap. At that point the session is spending longer scanning its own history than doing protocol work, and it is holding more memory than the rest of the router combined.

## Why it survived

Every long-lived session gets slow and nothing gets *fast*, so no test times out and no threshold trips. The only observable is throughput decay on exactly the sessions doing the most work.

## Do

Bound the set. The window only has to be as wide as a packet number can legitimately be re-sent, which is what the ACK and the resend timer already define — a duplicate outside the window is not a duplicate, it is a number the peer has already moved past.

- [ ] The set is bounded, and the bound is derived from something the protocol already states rather than picked as a round number.
- [ ] Duplicate suppression is still correct for any packet the peer could resend.
- [ ] A test that pushes a long run of packets and asserts the set does not grow past its bound. This is the test that would have caught it.
- [ ] A counter or log line when a packet number arrives outside the window, so an out-of-window retransmit is visible rather than silently processed as new.
- [ ] The resend path is checked: a packet still in `out_pkts` awaiting an ACK must not be dropped by the same bound.

add.issue.name: URGENT: a stuck NTCP2 connection can block the peer manager forever

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## Question

None — this is a defect, and it has the largest blast radius of anything found: **one** wedged connection can freeze I2NP ingress for **every** peer.

`i2p_ntcp2_conn:send/2` hands the payload to the connection process and then waits for a `{send_done, Ref}` reply with **no timeout clause**. The caller is `i2p_peer:send_i2np/3`, which runs inside `i2p_peer` — a single `gen_server`, one instance for the whole router. Every NTCP2 message the router sends therefore has an unbounded synchronous wait inside the one process every inbound message from every connection has to pass through.

## Measured

Called against a process that never replies, `i2p_ntcp2_conn:send/2` was **still blocked after 3000 ms** and would have blocked indefinitely. The wait has no bound to hit.

## Two distinct faults, both on this path

1. **Unbounded wait.** No timeout, so a connection process that is slow rather than dead — busy with a burst of AEAD, or blocked in the socket write because the peer's TCP window is full — stalls the peer manager for as long as it likes.
2. **Head-of-line within one connection.** The connection's data loop handles messages in arrival order in a single receive. A send therefore queues behind every inbound frame already buffered, so a connection with a deep receive queue makes the peer manager wait on inbound work it has no interest in.

SSU2 does not have this problem: its send entry point is a cast. The asymmetry is why this survives — a session that is merely busy degrades, and an NTCP2 one freezes.

## Do

- [ ] The peer manager never performs an unbounded wait on a connection process.
- [ ] Head-of-line ordering within a connection is removed, or bounded and recorded as an accepted trade-off.
- [ ] A stall has a defined outcome: something is logged or counted, and the connection's state reflects that it stopped accepting sends.
- [ ] The two transports are symmetric on the send path, so "make the busy one slower to fix" is no longer a reason to leave a defect in one of them.
- [ ] A test that stalls a connection process and asserts the peer manager keeps handling messages from every other peer. That test is the deliverable as much as the fix is.

add.issue.name: The NTCP2 listener accepts one inbound connection per second

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## Question

None — this is a defect, and a measured one.

`i2p_ntcp2_listener` is a hand-rolled `proc_lib` accept loop. It waits on a **1-second receive timeout** for its control messages (`port`, `address`, `stop`) and only calls `gen_tcp:accept` when that timeout expires. So the accept happens at most once per second, and the remaining connections sit in the kernel's accept queue.

## Measured

Six inbound TCP connections opened simultaneously, then the listen socket's accept-queue depth read from `/proc/net/tcp` every 500 ms:

| time | still unaccepted |
|---|---|
| +0 ms | 6 |
| +1011 ms | 5 |
| +2019 ms | 4 |
| +3028 ms | 3 |
| +4036 ms | 2 |
| +5046 ms | 1 |
| +6057 ms | 0 |

Six connections took 6.06 seconds. The rate is exactly one per second, which is the receive timeout, not a load effect.

## Why it matters

Inbound dials are how a router's peer set grows, and how it recovers after a restart. At one per second a peer churn event converges in minutes, and a router whose peers all die at once rebuilds its set at one peer per second. It is also the difference between "we are connected" and "we are connected in the next minute", which is exactly the kind of thing the status view is supposed to make legible.

## Do

- [ ] Accept is no longer rate-limited by the control-message poll.
- [ ] The control messages stay answered promptly — the timeout exists for them, so whatever replaces it has to answer them faster than a second.
- [ ] The listen socket is handed over to a connection process without a window in which a data-phase frame arrives at the wrong owner. That handover is already subtle and commented; a fix that loses it would be worse than the throttle.
- [ ] A test that opens a batch of inbound connections and asserts they are accepted within a stated bound. Assert the bound, not a sleep.

add.issue.name: The SSU2 listener does per-connection work in the shared socket owner

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## Question

How much of the work in front of an SSU2 connection is actually that connection's, and how much is every connection's?

The answer today: the shared listener does a lot of it. There is one listener process per bound address, it owns the only UDP socket, and on the way in and out of every datagram it does work that belongs to one session.

## What it does that belongs to a session

**Classification repeats itself.** Resolving a datagram's owner runs the long-header unmask up to three times: once in the initial classification, once when no session or pending endpoint claimed it, and once more in the handshake fallback. Each unmask is three raw ChaCha20 passes and two XORs.

**Measured, per 1472-byte datagram:** one long-header unmask is **2.38 µs**. A full AEAD decrypt of the same datagram — the actual work the session exists to do — is **1.40 µs**. So the shared listener spends roughly five times the crypto of the real work before handing the datagram to the process that will actually process it.

**The Charlie role runs inline.** Responding as Charlie to an out-of-session peer test is a role, and a per-connection one: decode the probe, build the reply, AEAD-encode it, send it. It executes in the listener, not in a connection process, because at that point there is no session to own it.

**The send path is centralised by necessity.** Only the listener can send, since it alone holds the socket, so every outbound datagram for every session is a cast into this one process — plus a byte count and up to four debug frames.

## Do

Preserve what the module doc argues for and change what it does. The routing order in that doc is a correctness fix, not a preference: reading the type byte first diverts roughly one SessionCreated in 256 into the Charlie responder, which drops it, and the peer dies with a handshake timeout an average of once every few thousand handshakes. Any simplification that reintroduces a type-byte-first decision undoes a bug that was expensive to find.

- [ ] Classification does the minimum crypto that is still exact, and the number of unmask passes per datagram is stated and justified in the module doc.
- [ ] The Charlie responder is either a per-connection process or a worker that cannot hold up datagram classification, and the answer says which and why.
- [ ] The measured per-datagram cost in the socket owner drops, and the measurement is recorded in the ticket so the improvement is checkable rather than asserted.
- [ ] The one-in-256 SessionCreated regression has a test.

add.issue.name: The tunnel path blocks on a NetDb call for every 1028-byte frame, and throws the answer away

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

Relaying a tunnel frame must not involve a round trip to the NetDb process.

Today `i2p_tunnel_relay:send_tunnel_data/2` looks up the next hop in the NetDb before handing the frame to the peer manager, and only uses the lookup to decide whether to send at all. The lookup is a **synchronous call into a gen_server**, and it returns a full RouterInfo that the caller immediately discards. It happens once per 1028-byte frame — so once per frame of every tunnel this router relays for the network, and once per frame of every message it injects.

Three costs, all of them per frame:

1. A cross-process call and reply, from inside the process that relays every tunnel.
2. A map lookup over the whole NetDb, which grows with the router's view of the network.
3. A **copy of a full RouterInfo across the process boundary**, roughly a kilobyte of map and binaries, to answer a yes/no question.

**Measured:** 1.39 µs on an *empty* NetDb, against a 1.28 µs floor for a bare call to a trivial server — so essentially all of it is the round trip, and it gets worse as the NetDb fills. The copy is not in that number and is pure waste.

## Why it matters

This is the coupling that makes the NetDb process a router-wide stall point. Anything slow in there — a signature verification, a disk write — is on the critical path of every relayed frame, and the next ticket is about both of those.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The existence check costs no cross-process round trip and copies no RouterInfo.
- [ ] Behaviour is unchanged when the next hop is unknown: the frame is dropped silently, because the peer manager owns reconnection.
- [ ] The NetDb keeps a single source of truth for "do we hold this RouterInfo". Two places must not be able to disagree about it.
- [ ] A test that asserts the relay path performs no blocking call per frame. The cheap way to make that testable is to make the check cheap enough to observe; the expensive way is an assertion about call counts, which is acceptable if the cheap option is not.
- [ ] The lookup that remains on the caller side of the process boundary, if any, is counted, so a drop is distinguishable from a send.

add.issue.name: The NetDb process runs signature verification and disk IO inline, and the tunnel path calls it synchronously

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y
Blocked by: #7GP4A4K is unrelated; this is blocked by the ticket removing the per-frame call

## What to build

A NetDb read must never wait for a NetDb write, and neither may wait for the disk.

`i2p_netdb_srv` is one gen_server holding the entire NetDb, and it does three classes of expensive work in its own process:

**Signature verification on every store.** Storing a RouterInfo decodes and verifies it inline. An Ed25519 verification is **90.01 µs measured** — roughly 65x the cost of the per-frame tunnel work it sits ahead of. A floodfill replication burst, or the 75-RouterInfo bundle a reseed delivers, is a run of those back to back.

**A full disk save every 15 minutes.** The autosave serialises the entire NetDb and writes it out inside the same process, on a timer, with nothing else running in it. On a real NetDb that is tens to hundreds of milliseconds during which no read is served.

**An expiry sweep every 30 minutes.** A full pass over routers and LeaseSets, same process.

## Why it matters

Today the tunnel path calls this process once per relayed frame, so all three stall tunnel relaying. The previous ticket removes that per-frame call, which is what makes this one tractable — but the work still belongs off the read path, because a lookup-driven read and a reseed-driven write should not be in the same queue at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A store does not block a concurrent read, and a read does not block a store.
- [ ] The disk write does not run in the process that serves reads.
- [ ] The expiry sweep does not run in the process that serves reads.
- [ ] Signature verification happens somewhere that is not a reader's critical path.
- [ ] A test that starts a save and asserts reads are still served, and one that issues a burst of stores and asserts reads are still served. Assert the read completed, not that it completed quickly.
- [ ] The 15-minute and 30-minute intervals stay configurable, and the answer says whether they should now be tuned against a router that is not blocking on them.

add.issue.name: Client sends block on the tunnel manager's call

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

A client sending a message must not wait on the tunnel manager's queue.

`i2p_tunnel_srv:send_via_outbound/3` is a synchronous call, and it is on the client send path: a SAM or streaming session that wants to send calls it and waits. Inside the call the tunnel manager fragments the message, pre-applies every hop's inverse layer, and hands each frame onward.

The consequences:

- **Every client session serialises behind every other one.** They are all waiting on one process.
- **They also serialise behind inbound work.** The same process is handling transit frames for the network and unwrapping its own inbound tunnels at the same time, so a client send's latency depends on how much transit the router happens to be carrying.
- **The cryptography is on the caller's clock.** The framing and layer work — measured at 6.74 µs per frame for the layer preparation alone over a 3-hop tunnel — happens before the caller is released.

## What it must not cost

The call returns `ok | error`, and callers care: `error` means no outbound tunnel with that ID is active. Whatever replaces the call has to keep that answer available, either by returning it or by reporting it as an event. Silently dropping the error would turn a routing fault into silence, which is the class of bug this board has already found twice.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A client send does not wait on unrelated tunnel work — neither another client's send nor transit for other routers.
- [ ] The `ok | error` answer survives, or its loss is replaced by an event that carries the same information.
- [ ] A message that cannot be injected is reported, so "my send vanished" is diagnosable.
- [ ] A test with two sessions and a busy tunnel manager asserts neither session's send is gated by the other's.

add.issue.name: Ship dirty-scheduler crypto flags

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

Tunnel cryptography must not run on the same schedulers as the router's message handling.

There is no `+sbwt` or `+sbwtdcpu` anywhere in the tree — not in the shipped `config/vm.args`, not in `rebar.config`. OTP 27 and later default both to `none`, so every cryptographic operation the router performs runs inline on a normal scheduler.

The per-frame costs, all measured, all of which land on normal schedulers:

- transit relay, one hop layer: **1.55 µs** per 1028-byte frame
- outbound injection, 3-hop tunnel: **6.74 µs** per frame
- inbound endpoint unwrap, 3 layers: **6.51 µs** per frame
- SSU2 long-header unmask, which the socket owner does up to three times per datagram: **2.38 µs** each

Those numbers are small individually and they are not the problem. The problem is that they execute on the schedulers also running the SSU2 listener, the peer manager, and the tunnel manager — the three processes everything else is waiting on. On a small router, relaying traffic for the network is arithmetic taken directly out of ingress.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The release ships crypto scheduler flags, and `just check` and `just dialyzer` still pass.
- [ ] The ticket records which OTP versions honour the flags and what the behavioural difference is, so a future reader is not left guessing whether they are load-bearing.
- [ ] The effect is measured, not asserted: ingress latency under synthetic transit load, before and after. If the measurement does not show a difference on the smallest supported host, that is a finding worth recording rather than a reason to skip the flags.
- [ ] The cost of the flags is stated — dirty schedulers are not free, and on a one-core host they are not an improvement.

add.issue.name: Per-datagram syscall and log allocation in the SSU2 hot path

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

The per-datagram overhead in front of an SSU2 session should be paid only when something is wrong.

Two costs sit on every datagram regardless of whether anything interesting happens.

**A syscall per datagram, in the single socket owner.** The listener drives the socket `{active, once}` and re-arms it with `inet:setopts` after each datagram. The intent is sound — a flood can then only starve itself instead of filling a mailbox — but the re-arm is a syscall in the one process that owns the socket and does the classification, and the socket is idle between finishing one datagram and re-arming.

**Argument construction before the level check.** `i2p_log:debug/2` allocates its metadata map on every call regardless of level, and the SSU2 data path eagerly builds a list of block kinds for every inbound datagram as an argument. The default level is `notice`, so nothing formats — the allocation is pure waste on the common path, and the block-kind list is the larger of the two because it walks the datagram's blocks.

## The trade-off to decide rather than assume

`{active, once}` is a real choice, not an oversight. `{active, true}` removes the syscall and lets the runtime deliver without one, at the cost of a mailbox that a flood can fill. Whichever way this goes, the answer should say what the bound on memory is, because that is the property the current design is buying.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The log level gates argument construction, not only formatting. A debug frame costs a level check on the hot path.
- [ ] The re-arm strategy is chosen deliberately and the choice is recorded with its memory bound.
- [ ] Neither change alters what the module doc says about classification order — the one-in-256 SessionCreated fix must survive a refactor of the hot path around it.
- [ ] The per-datagram cost in the socket owner is measured before and after, and both numbers are in the ticket.

add.issue.name: The event bus is a synchronous call on the data path

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

Announcing a fact must never be able to stall the work that produced it.

`i2p_events:notify/1` is a `gen_event:notify`, which is a call to the manager process. The manager invokes handler callbacks in its own process, so it is not just a queue — a handler that is slow holds the manager, and a notifier is waiting on the manager.

That puts it on the data path. The relay calls it when it denies a transit build. The peer manager calls it on every connect, disconnect, and failed connect. The session calls it when a peer test resolves. Every one of those is a caller that is in the middle of moving a message and now cannot proceed until a subscriber finishes.

The subscribers are outside the router: the status service attaches over Erlang distribution, and ADR 0001 makes that the intended arrangement. So the router's transit relay is synchronously coupled to a presentation app it was designed never to need to know about.

## The decision to make

Whether a handler is slow should be impossible, or merely survivable. `i2p_events:notify/1` already returns `ok` unconditionally and discards delivery failures, so best-effort is the intent — but the current mechanism is not best-effort, it is best-effort-after-blocking. Pick one and write it down:

- **bounded**: the manager answers within a bound, so a wedged handler costs a bounded stall, or
- **detached**: the announce is handed off and the notifier moves on, which means a notifier crash can lose a fact, and that has to be an accepted statement rather than an accident.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A slow or wedged subscriber cannot stall the relay path or the peer manager.
- [ ] Delivery semantics are stated: guaranteed, best-effort, or bounded — and the mechanism matches the statement.
- [ ] Losing a fact is either impossible or counted, so "the subscriber was too slow" is distinguishable from "nothing happened".
- [ ] A test that attaches a handler which blocks, and asserts relay work still completes.

add.issue.name: Connection admission takes a node-wide distributed lock

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

The connection cap must hold under concurrent dials without a router-wide mutex.

Admission for all three client-facing connection kinds — NTCP2, SSU2, and SAM sessions — is a count-then-start, and the count has to be atomic with the start or the cap is advisory. Each supervisor does this by wrapping the check and the `supervisor:start_child` in `global:trans/2`.

`global:trans` is a distributed lock. On a single node it is a call to the `global` server process, which every admission in the router serialises through, and it stays that way on a node with no peers. The child count it guards is itself read by walking the supervisor's children, so the critical section covers a supervision-tree traversal as well.

This is on connection establishment, not per packet, so it is not a throughput ceiling. It is a router-wide lock on the one operation that is bursty at exactly the wrong moment: after a restart, or when a peer set is rebuilt, or when a floodfill replication burst brings in a wave of new peers — which is when many handshakes complete at once.

## Do

- [ ] The cap still holds: concurrent dials cannot exceed it. This is the property, and it is not negotiable in exchange for removing the lock.
- [ ] Either admission needs no node-wide lock, or the lock is kept and justified in the module doc — a node-local counter, or a counter the supervisor owns rather than one derived by walking its children.
- [ ] A test that starts many dials concurrently and asserts the resulting connection count never exceeds the cap. A barrier, not a sleep.
- [ ] Whether the lock's scope should include the SAM supervisor is answered rather than assumed; it is a different resource from a peer connection.

add.issue.name: How does the tunnel path come off a single process?

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y
Blocked by: #W46KMT8, #PPW41Y4, #G9HZK8F

## Question

Every tunnel message this router handles — relaying somebody else's, injecting its own client's, unwrapping its own inbound — is executed by **one process**. `i2p_tunnel_srv` is a single `gen_server`, one instance for the router, a `permanent` child of the top supervisor. It is on the critical path of the network's traffic and of every client session simultaneously, and it holds all the pool state.

The measured cost of the work it serialises, per frame:

- transit relay, one hop layer: **1.55 µs** per 1028-byte frame
- outbound injection through a 3-hop tunnel: **6.74 µs**
- inbound endpoint unwrap, 3 layers: **6.51 µs**
- SSU2 long-header unmask the socket owner does up to three times per datagram: **2.38 µs** each

Those are not large numbers. The question is what the ceiling is once they are the *only* thing the process does, and the answer is that the router's transit service and every client session contend for one process with no ordering guarantee between them. A client send waits on transit for other routers. A transit frame waits on a client send's fragmentation and layer work.

## What to decide

The three tickets this is blocked by remove the worst couplings first: the per-frame NetDb call, the NetDb's inline verification and disk IO, and the blocking client send. Doing those first is what makes the remaining question tractable — the design should be settled against the post-fix shape, not the current one.

So decide:

- **What is the unit of work per process.** Per tunnel, per pool (client / exploratory / transit), or per direction (inbound / outbound)? Each gives a different failure domain and a different answer to "what is the blast radius when one dies". A per-tunnel process is the finest, but a 3-hop client tunnel is 3 processes and a transit router holds up to `transit_max_tunnels` of them.
- **What stays central.** Pool selection, LeaseSet publication, the length demands, and the status view all read the same maps. If the state shards, the status view has to aggregate, and the read API is a public contract that only changes additively within a version — so the aggregate has to be assembled from shards without changing its shape.
- **What a shard's death means.** Today the process is `permanent` and its death takes the whole tunnel subsystem with it; the store-type defect already on the board shows what that costs. A shard that dies takes one tunnel instead. Is that the right granularity for supervision, and does a client's tunnel silently rebuilding become a client-visible event?
- **Whether transit is separated from client traffic at all.** The exploratory pool already exists to stop lookup gossip competing with client traffic, and the module doc says so. If transit gets its own process, does the client pool get its own, and does anything still share a scheduler?
- **What this costs the state view.** `i2p_status_data:view/0` is a single-call snapshot that a presentation app renders. Sharding the state that feeds it is a change to how that snapshot is assembled, and the answer has to say how it stays a single call.

## Notes

The two related questions this touches are already settled elsewhere and are not reopened here: that the core never renders ([ADR 0001](https://github.com/freke/i2per/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-data-only-core-with-presentation-apps.md)), and that the read API's shape is fixed for a version ([the telemetry contract](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/3H11881)).

This is a fork with a blast radius past its own ticket, so it is a decision to make rather than a change to make. If the answer turns out to be "shard later, measure first", that is a legitimate outcome and the ticket should record what would have to be true to revisit it.

add.issue.comment.md:
## Routing-path investigation — 1/3: the finding, and Tier 1

A pass over the message path (datagram in, message out) produced twelve tickets, all tagged `routing-path`, all in Todo and ordered. Every number in them is measured on this tree, not estimated.

**What this batch establishes that the board did not have: the connection model is sound.** One process per NTCP2 connection, one per SSU2 session, one per SAM session — all `temporary` children of `one_for_one` supervisors, verified by killing a connection and watching the listener and its siblings survive. There is already a test for that on NTCP2 and it passes. The problem is not the per-connection processes. It is the three singleton processes every one of them passes through on the way in and out.

### Tier 1 — local availability, ahead of all 0.2.0 planning

**[#7GP4A4K](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/7GP4A4K) — SSU2 received-packet set grows without bound and is scanned linearly.**
Self-triggering: no adversary, no load spike. Any long-lived SSU2 session slows until it stops. The set of received packet numbers is only ever prepended to, and the membership test that reads it is a linear scan, so the cost per datagram grows with every datagram the session has ever received. Measured 1.41 µs at 1k packets, 223 µs at 100k, 1.6 ms at 1M, at 16 bytes of heap per packet received. Quadratic, and nothing ever times out — which is exactly why no test catches it.

**[#G4TF5RT](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/G4TF5RT) — a stuck NTCP2 connection can block the peer manager forever.**
Largest blast radius of anything found. The send path waits for a reply with no timeout clause, and it is called from inside the one process every peer's inbound traffic passes through. One slow peer — a congested path, a full TCP window — stops I2NP for every peer. Verified: still blocked at 3 s against a process that never answers. SSU2 does not have it, which is why it survived.

**[#ZYQ227K](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/ZYQ227K) — the NTCP2 listener accepts one inbound connection per second.**
Measured and unconditional. The accept loop polls its control messages on a 1 s timeout, so it accepts once per second regardless of load; six simultaneous inbound connections took 6.06 s to drain, read from the kernel's accept queue. This is the rate peer sets grow at and recover at.

These rank **below [#XNBSG6A](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/XNBSG6A) and [#JDQ8E3Q](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/JDQ8E3Q)**, which stay first: their blast radius is the network's rather than ours, and XNBSG6A is reachable from a lookup reply. They rank **above all 0.2.0 feature work**, because a router that cannot carry traffic has nothing to observe.

### Tier 2 — the couplings on the routing path

Ordered so each removes a whole-router stall point, and so the design question comes last, against an already-simplified path.

**[#W46KMT8](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/W46KMT8) → [#PPW41Y4](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/PPW41Y4)** are a pair and must run in that order.

And the NetDb does 90 µs Ed25519 verifications on store, plus a full-NetDb serialise-and-write every 15 minutes and an expiry sweep every 30, all in the same process. Remove the call first; the remaining NetDb work then only hurts NetDb users.

**[#G9HZK8F](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/G9HZK8F)** is the same shape on the client side: a client send is a blocking call, so every session waits behind every other session *and* behind transit for other routers.

[#7YP3QZ4](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/7YP3QZ4) is the ticket that makes those two distinguishable, and it is the instrument for everything in this tier. The byte counters — [#VZVB7X8](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/VZVB7X8) at the transport boundary and [#3846833](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/3846833) at the transit relay — are the other half, and they are what tells you whether a Tier 2 fix actually worked rather than merely appearing to.

add.issue.comment.md:
### Tier 3 — per-packet overhead

**[#VXRH456](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/VXRH456)** first, despite being nearly trivial: there are no crypto scheduler flags anywhere in the tree, so on OTP 27+ every tunnel operation runs on the same schedulers as the three processes everything else is waiting on. The individual costs are small — 1.55 µs per relayed hop layer, 6.74 µs per injected frame over a 3-hop tunnel. The contention is the point.

**[#4F1M83V](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/4F1M83V)** next: the event bus is a synchronous call, and a subscriber is by design a separate application the core must not be coupled to ([ADR 0001](https://github.com/freke/i2per/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-data-only-core-with-presentation-apps.md)). So a slow status service can currently stall transit relaying. The decision here is whether a slow handler should be *impossible* or merely *survivable* — `i2p_events:notify/1` already returns `ok` unconditionally, so best-effort is the intent, but the mechanism is best-effort-after-blocking.

**[#YNBT5ZD](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/YNBT5ZD) and [#XZTYAVX](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/XZTYAVX)** overlap and are candidates for a merge — both are per-datagram work in front of an SSU2 session. Measured: the shared listener spends about **five times the crypto of the session's own decrypt** on classification before handing a datagram over, and the Charlie peer-test role runs in the listener rather than in a connection process. Left as two tickets deliberately: the classification reduction is a small crypto saving, the Charlie-responder move is a structural change with a regression to preserve, and the one-in-256 `SessionCreated` misroute is the expensive bug in that module's history. Say the word if you would rather have one ticket.

**[#41D5PFF](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/41D5PFF)** last. It is a router-wide lock on connection *establishment*, not a per-packet ceiling, and it bites exactly when a peer set is being rebuilt — the same moment [#ZYQ227K](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/ZYQ227K) is already slowing things down.

### What the measurements ruled out

Recorded so nobody re-derives it. **Parsing is not a bottleneck**: framing decode and I2NP decode together cost **0.06 µs** per message, so the singleton `i2p_peer` is not limited by its own work. `i2p_stats:add/2` is a lock-free `counters:add` off `persistent_term` and is correct as designed. And the NTCP2 process-isolation story is genuinely good — which is what makes the three singleton bottlenecks worth fixing rather than the per-connection model worth doubting.

### A board problem worth naming

Every ticket on this board, including the twelve just filed, sits in the **Done** lane with `isClosed` false. The lanes were set up as a kanban and are not being used as one, so the board currently carries no ordering information at all — a reader has to infer priority from title prefixes and timestamps. The ordering in these three comments is real, but it lives in the comments rather than in the board. Worth a cleanup pass before the next session has to guess.

add.issue.name: The NTCP2 receive path reimplemented frame decryption, and the two copies have diverged

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

One implementation of NTCP2 frame decryption, and a statement of which module owns it.

`i2p_framing` presents a symmetric pair, `encrypt_frame/4` and `decrypt_frame/4`. Only the first is used. The send path calls it; the receive path goes through `i2p_stream:push/2`, which does its own length deobfuscation and its own AEAD open. `decrypt_frame/4` has no caller anywhere outside its own moduledoc example.

**They are no longer the same function, which is the part that matters.**

- `decrypt_frame/4` treats a length that disagrees with the available bytes as a malformed frame and returns `error`.
- The copy in `i2p_stream` treats it as a frame that has not fully arrived, buffers it, and waits for more bytes.

That is the right behaviour for a stream, and the wrong behaviour for a single-frame API — so the unused one is not a copy waiting to be wired up, it is a copy that was outgrown. Which means the module advertises a symmetry it does not have, and a reader comparing the two has no way to know which is authoritative.

## Why it survived

Both halves are covered. `i2p_framing` is tested through `decrypt_frame/4`, and the NTCP2 connection tests cover the receive path through `i2p_stream`. So the suite is green over a function nothing calls and a function everything calls, and neither test notices the other exists.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Exactly one implementation of NTCP2 frame decryption.
- [ ] If `i2p_framing` keeps both halves, `i2p_stream` calls `decrypt_frame/4` and the partial-frame buffering lives in one place. If it keeps only the send half, `decrypt_frame/4` is deleted and the module doc says the receive direction belongs to `i2p_stream`.
- [ ] A test that would fail if the two ever diverged again — or, if one is deleted, a test that the surviving one covers the buffering contract it now owns.
- [ ] The module doc states which module owns which direction, so the next reader is not left inferring it from call sites.

add.issue.name: The Noise XX ratchet and ElG2 surface is exhaustively tested and never called

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

A decision about eleven exported functions that no production path reaches, made explicitly rather than by default.

The surface: `noise_initialize/0`, `dh_initialize/2`, `dh_ratchet_tagset/2`, `symmetric_ratchet/1`, `session_tag_chain_init/1`, `session_tag_chain_step/2`, `session_reply_tagset/1`, `elligator2_encode/1,2,3`, `elligator2_decode/1`, `x25519_keygen_elg2/0` — roughly 250 lines implementing the Noise XX handshake ratchet and ElG2 key representation.

**What production actually uses** is three functions: `noise_n_initialize/0`, `noise_n_encrypt/5`, `noise_n_decrypt/6`, and only from the ECIES tunnel layer. The SSU2 handshake does not use the ratchet at all — it has its own initialisation and its own mixing.

## Why this is worse than dead code

The test suite covers this surface thoroughly, including ElG2 vectors taken from a Java implementation and a full ratchet step test. So `just check` reports protocol coverage for a component the router never runs. That is the failure mode the map warns about in a different guise: a green gate that certifies something untrue.

There is also a naming hazard sitting in the middle of it. `noise_initialize/0` is dead and `noise_n_initialize/0` is live, one character apart, with opposite liveness, both exported, both meaning "start a Noise handshake". A reader has no way to tell which one the code is supposed to call.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision, recorded: the surface is either wired into a real handshake or removed. It does not stay in its current state, where it is neither.
- [ ] If removed, the tests that cover it go with it, and the suite stops reporting coverage for a component that does not run.
- [ ] The `noise_initialize/0` versus `noise_n_initialize/0` hazard is resolved either way. Renaming, or removing one, both count; leaving both does not.
- [ ] If it is wired in rather than removed, the answer says which handshake adopts it and what the existing hand-rolled initialisation in the SSU2 module becomes.
- [ ] ElG2 in particular is answered, not deferred: either a caller appears or the encoding goes, because an unused key representation is a protocol claim nobody is making.

add.issue.name: i2p_sam_proxy is test scaffolding that ships in the release and is documented as a feature

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

The release should not contain a test fixture, and the public API reference should not describe one as a product.

`i2p_sam_proxy` is a 324-line HTTP GET proxy that fetches URLs through the SAM v3 STREAM interface. Its only caller in the entire repository is the SAM test suite.

Two things follow from that:

**It ships.** It lives in `apps/i2per/src`, so it is compiled into the application and included in the relx artifact. A test fixture is in the operator's release.

**It is documented as a feature.** The generated API reference lists it among the modules with a one-line description reading as a capability. Anyone reading the documentation — including whoever writes the release notes — would reasonably conclude the router has an HTTP proxy. It does not. It has a test fixture.

The second is the worse of the two. A module in `src/` is a claim; the docs turn that claim into a promise.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The module lives where it belongs — the test tree — or is deleted and the test rewritten against a fixture that is.
- [ ] The API reference is regenerated and no longer describes a fixture as a capability.
- [ ] The release artifact is checked for test-only modules, so the next one is caught rather than found. The release gate is the natural place, and the standing preference on this project is that a property nobody tests is a property that quietly stops holding.
- [ ] If it is kept in `src/` deliberately, the reason is written down and the documentation stops implying it is a feature.

add.issue.name: i2p_streaming's field accessors are read through and written around

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

One way to name a streaming packet's fields, enforced rather than observed.

`i2p_streaming` exposes thirteen one-line accessors over the packet fields. Readers use them, which is reasonable. Writers do not: the stream connection module builds packets with raw map keys — `max_packet_size =>`, `resend_delay =>`, `payload =>` — spelled literally at three construction sites.

So the accessors give the appearance of a single place that knows the wire field names, and the construction sites are that second place. Renaming a field in the type breaks the readers at compile time and the writers at runtime, which is the worst of both: a field rename looks safe and is not.

A map is unchecked by construction, so this is the case where a type change is what would actually enforce the rule rather than merely document it.

## Why it matters beyond tidiness

The 0.2.0 map's standing preference is that data is never duplicated and one place is the source. This is that rule with the enforcement missing — and it sits on the client's message path, where a silently malformed packet is a stream that stops working for a reason nothing records.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A packet is constructed in one place. Either the module owns construction, or the type is a record or tuple and the field names are checked at compile time.
- [ ] No construction site outside the owning module spells a wire field as a literal map key.
- [ ] A test that fails if a field is added to the type without a corresponding reader and writer — written against the type rather than a hand-written list, so the type stays the single source.
- [ ] The answer says which of the three shapes was chosen and why, since a record and a construction-function are different commitments.

add.issue.name: Is the i2p_log checklist apparatus still the right shape at this size?

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## Question

Is the checklist apparatus still the right shape at the size the tree has become, or has it outgrown what it was built to prevent?

This is a design question, not a defect, and the answer is the maintainer's — the module is [ADR 0002](https://github.com/freke/i2per/blob/main/docs/adr/0002-the-logging-floor-the-bus-is-the-instrument.md)'s explicit design and nothing here says it failed. What follows is the bill for it.

**What it costs.** `i2p_log` is 494 lines for what started as a level setter, and 101 of those are the module doc explaining why the module exists. It exports twelve functions. The load-bearing part beyond the level setter is `checklist/0` — seven declared facts, each with a level and an instrument — plus `emit/3`, which refuses any fact the checklist does not declare, plus `fact_names/0`, plus a test pinning the shipped `config/sys.config` level to `default_level/0` so a release cannot start at one verbosity and become another.

**What that buys.** A log line cannot be written at a level nobody chose, and a fact carried on the event bus cannot also be written to the log, so the overlap ADR 0002 warns about is prevented by the code rather than by a reviewer noticing. Both are real.

**Where the cost lands.** Three places, and they are not equally weighted:

1. **The gate is partly structural theatre.** The checklist declares rows whose instrument is the bus, and `emit/3` raises on them. So half the declared rows exist to be refused by the only function that reads them. That is a table documenting an invariant the type system could state, at the price of a runtime error instead of a compile error.
2. **The indirection is on every call site.** There are 65 debug frames alone. Each is a call into a wrapper whose body is one `logger` call, and — this is the part that interacts with the routing-path work — the wrapper allocates its metadata map before the level check, so the level gates the formatting but not the allocation.
3. **The two-entry-point split is real complexity.** `emit/3` is gated and `debug/2` is not, and the module doc argues at length why both must exist. That argument is good. It is also 40 lines of prose defending a distinction a reader has to hold in their head before they can add a log line.

## Decide

- **Keep it as is.** Defensible, and the ADR is the reason. The cost is understood and paid on purpose.
- **Keep the gate, drop the ceremony around it.** The checklist stays load-bearing; the bus rows, the `fact_names/0` accessor, and the prose defending the two entry points go. Smallest change that keeps the property.
- **Move the gate to compile time.** The instrument distinction becomes part of the fact type, so a bus-carried fact cannot reach a log-emitting function at all. Bigger change, removes the runtime error class entirely.
- **Drop the checklist, keep the level setter.** The honest floor is a hot level and an allowlist. Loses the "a fact nobody listed is a fact nobody will look for" property, which is the thing ADR 0002 was written to get.

## What is not in question

The allowlist for loggable configuration keys stays — it is a denylist's worth of protection against printing a private key, and it is cheap. The hot `log_level` key stays; it is the right shape for a 3am change. And the test pinning the shipped `sys.config` level to the module default stays whatever else happens, because a release that disagrees with itself about its own verbosity is a bug with no other symptom.

## A note on the interaction

The routing-path work found that the debug entry point allocates before it checks the level, on the SSU2 per-datagram path. Whatever this ticket decides, that allocation should end up behind the level check. If the answer here is "keep it as is", the allocation still needs fixing and it belongs to the routing-path ticket rather than to this one.

add.issue.name: A peer whose SSU2 address does not answer costs 20 seconds before NTCP2 is tried

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

A dial that does not spend twenty seconds proving UDP is dead before it tries TCP.

## Measured, not estimated

The slowest test in the Common Test run is `i2p_peer_transport_suite:transport_falls_back_to_ntcp2`, at **11 seconds**. It is not a slow test. It is measuring this.

The test advertises a peer with an SSU2 address that nothing answers, and its own comment says what happens:

> The remote advertises an SSU2 address nothing answers. The SSU2 handshake times out (the fixed ~20s connect budget), the dial falls back to NTCP2, and the same queued work completes over TCP. *Slow by design, hence the explicit 60s timetrap on this scenario.*

Confirmed in source: the SSU2 connect path waits 20 seconds for a session, and the peer manager's transport selection is **serial** — the dial prefers SSU2, and the module doc states the handshake "blocks until it succeeds or fails; on failure (SessionCreated timeout, protocol error, or an attempt at a dead SSU2 port) the dial falls back to NTCP2."

So on any path where UDP does not come back — a stateful firewall, a middlebox, a lossy or congested route — **every peer costs up to twenty seconds of dead time before TCP is attempted at all.** The test is the only place in the tree that makes that cost visible, and it is currently written as an accepted 60-second-budget scenario rather than as a fault.

## Why it is worse than twenty seconds of latency

**It compounds with the rest of the routing-path work.** A peer set rebuild is exactly when many dials happen at once, and that is the same moment [ZYQ227K](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/ZYQ227K) is already accepting inbound connections at one per second. A router restarting onto a live network pays the full budget per peer before its first contact, and a peer that flaps re-pays it on every attempt because the fallback is not retried in the other order.

**The failure is indistinguishable from slowness.** Nothing measures it. The peer manager's own backoff only starts once a connect has *failed*, so a dial parked in a 20-second SSU2 wait is not in backoff, is not failing, and is not counted anywhere.

## What to decide

The shape of the fix is a real fork, not a tuning knob:

- **Race them.** Start both, use whichever establishes first, drop the other. Fastest when both work, and it removes the serial dependency entirely — at the cost of two handshakes per peer on the happy path, which is crypto the peer pays for too.
- **Stagger, Happy-Eyeballs style.** Start SSU2, start NTCP2 after a short delay, prefer SSU2 if it wins. Bounds the cost without doubling the happy path. Needs a number for the delay and a reason for it.
- **Probe first.** Decide the transport from a cheap reachability signal before committing to a handshake. Cheapest, and it needs a signal that is actually predictive — which, given that the whole point of the peer test is that reachability is only knowable by trying, is the hard part.
- **Shorten the budget.** Smallest change and it only moves the constant. Worth saying plainly that on its own this trades a twenty-second stall for a shorter one and makes the fallback *more* likely to fire on a merely slow path rather than a dead one.

Whichever is chosen, the answer should say what happens to a peer that publishes **both** transports and is reachable on only one, because that is the case the current design handles worst and the case a real network produces constantly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The cost of reaching a peer that answers on NTCP2 but not on SSU2 is bounded by something other than the SSU2 handshake budget, and the bound is stated.
- [ ] A test asserts the bound. Not that a fallback eventually happens — that it happens within a stated window. The existing test asserts the 60-second timetrap is not exceeded, which is a statement about the test rather than the product.
- [ ] The dial policy for a peer publishing both transports is written down, including the case where only one is reachable.
- [ ] A dial parked waiting on an unresponsive transport is visible — counted or logged — so a twenty-second stall is distinguishable from a slow one. This is the same class as the 0.2.0 lookup-failed-by-reason work: a fault with no counter is a fault nobody can diagnose.
- [ ] Whatever is chosen, the answer says what it does to the happy path, not only what it does to the failure path.

add.issue.name: Three test-suite costs, and one silent coverage gap

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

A unit-test run that is quick enough to be run often, and a gate that fails when a suite stops running.

## Measured

**EUnit: 14.1 s, 837 tests.** Two items are 46% of it.

**CT: 2 m 19 s wall, but only 26 s of CPU** — the run is 80% waiting. The distribution is extremely skewed, which is the useful part:

- **201 of 262 cases finish in under a second** and account for effectively none of the wall time.
- **19 cases take 2 s or more and account for 65 s — 61% of the whole run.**
- 9 suites cost 0.00 s, and `i2p_tunnel_srv_SUITE` runs 43 cases in 2.0 s at a 46 ms mean.

So this is not a systemic slowness problem. The infrastructure is already capable of being fast, and the cost is concentrated in a handful of places. That is worth recording because the obvious conclusion — "the test suite is slow" — is wrong, and acting on it would mean rewriting suites that are already fine.

## The three items

**1. One test is 36% of the EUnit run, and the cost is a hardcoded constant.**
`derived_figures_appear_after_two_readings` takes **5.02 s**. It needs two readings to derive a rate, and the poll interval is `?POLL_MS = 5000`, hardcoded. The test's own comment is right that its wait is a condition and not a sleep — the *interval* is the cost, not the test.

The fix already has a precedent in this tree: `i2p_netdb_srv` reads its autosave and expiry intervals from the application environment with a macro default. Make the poll interval injectable the same way. The test drops to roughly ten milliseconds with the same assertion, and stops depending on poll alignment.

**2. Two RSA-4096 keys per test run.**
`i2p_su3_tests` memoises its keys — the author already did the hard part — but 4096 bits is over-specified for tests that check container encoding and certificate validity. Measured on this machine: RSA-4096 **531 ms**, RSA-2048 25 ms, RSA-1024 9 ms. Two keys is about **1.06 s** of a 14.1 s run.

Dropping to 2048 costs roughly 50 ms and removes a variance source, which matters more than the time: 4096-bit keygen time varies widely between machines, and a test whose duration is dominated by prime search is a flake waiting for a loaded CI runner.

**3. Nothing enforces that the Common Test suite list matches the suites on disk.**
All 26 suites are currently listed — verified. But `rebar.config` carries a comment saying to keep the list in sync when adding or removing a suite, and **no test checks it.** Add a `_SUITE.erl`, forget the list, and it silently never runs while `just check` stays green.

That is worse than a missing test, because a missing test is visible and this one is invisible. It is also the same failure shape the 0.2.0 map already records about 0.1.0's harm-avoidance property: a thing that quietly stops holding because nothing is watching it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The poll interval is injectable, following the pattern already in `i2p_netdb_srv`, with the shipped default unchanged.
- [ ] No test generates a key larger than the property under test needs, and the reason is written where the size is chosen.
- [ ] A test reads `rebar.config` and the test directory and asserts the two agree, modulo the interop suite that is deliberately excluded. It should name the excluded one explicitly, so the exclusion is a decision the test records rather than a gap it tolerates.
- [ ] Adding a suite file without listing it **fails the gate.** That is the part that matters; the check existing is not sufficient on its own.
- [ ] EUnit and CT wall times are re-measured and the before-and-after recorded here, so the next person is not re-deriving which tests are slow.

## What is not in question

The test infrastructure is good and should not be touched as part of this. Only 19 `timer:sleep` calls exist across 75 test files, and the ones that do are principled. `i2p_ct_helpers:events_from/1` barriers on a known event announced after the work, precisely because a notify call returning is not a delivery guarantee, and accumulates rather than discards so negative assertions work. `no_timer_is_scheduled_test` observes with a trace rather than waiting and hoping. `catch` never wraps an assertion anywhere, and 38 files use `try...after` for cleanup.

Do not "fix" any of that.

add.issue.comment.md:
## Correction: item 2 is wrong, and acting on it would break reseed verification

I put this up as "4096 is over-specified, drop to 2048". That is false, and the failure to find it was mine. I changed the fixture to 2048 and the suite went red immediately, which is the correct outcome and the reason this note exists rather than a silent edit.

**`i2p_su3` only accepts a 4096-bit RSA signature.** The decoder rejects any other signature length outright, and the encoder pads to that length:

- the declared signature type must be `0x0006` (RSA-SHA512-4096); anything else is `unsupported_signature_type`
- the declared signature length must be exactly 512 bytes; anything else is `bad_signature_length`
- on encode, the signature is left-padded to 512

512 bytes is the modulus size of a 4096-bit key. **There is no other key size that round-trips through this codec.** So the 4096 in the test fixture is not over-specification — it is the only size the product accepts, and the fixture author sized the key to the codec rather than arbitrarily. Dropping it to 2048 produces a file the router itself declares malformed.

The observed failure is worth recording because it shows the check is real and in the right order: the content-type assertion in that case was passing for the wrong reason. The decode failed at signature length before it ever reached the content-type check, so a 2048-bit fixture would have produced `bad_signature_length` while the case under test is about a wrong content type.

**So the ~1.06 s stands.** It is the price of exercising the real verification path, and it is not removable by changing a number. The options that remain are the ones below, and none of them is "use a smaller key".

- **A checked-in fixture key and certificate.** Removes the keygen entirely — the test cost becomes zero rather than 1.06 s — at the cost of a PEM in the repository. This is the only option that actually recovers the time, and it is the ordinary answer for a test that needs a stable signing identity. It also removes the variance, which matters more than the time: 4096-bit keygen is dominated by prime search and varies widely between machines.
- **Share one key across all four sites.** There are four memoised 4096 keygens in the tree (the SU3 unit suite, the reseed unit suite, the boot suite, and the reseed service suite). One shared memoised fixture in the existing test-helper module would mean one keygen per run instead of four, and would make the four sites agree on one identity by construction rather than by four independent copies.
- **Leave it.** 1.06 s of a 14.1 s unit run is not worth a committed private key if nobody minds the number.

Whichever is chosen, the acceptance criterion "no test generates a key larger than the property under test needs" needs rewording — as written it reads as licence to shrink this one, and shrinking it is wrong. The criterion should be about *duplicate* keygens, not about key size.

Items 1 and 3 of this ticket are unaffected and stand as written.

add.issue.comment.md:
## This is a memory-exhaustion bug, not a performance one — measured

I filed this as quadratic CPU. That undersells it. A second pass measuring memory per connection puts a number on it, and the number changes what kind of ticket this is.

## Measured

The set of received packet numbers costs **exactly 16 bytes per packet received** — a cons cell is two words, and the packet numbers are small integers, so they are immediates and add nothing. Nothing is ever freed: the set is initialised empty during the handshake and only ever prepended to.

| packets received | bytes held | vs a ~15 KB connection process |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 16 KB | 105% |
| 10,000 | 160 KB | 1,051% |
| 100,000 | 1.6 MB | 10,506% |
| 1,000,000 | 16 MB | 105,056% |

On **one** session at 1,000 packets/second: **937 KB per minute, 54 MB per hour, 1 GB per day.**

## Why this is a different kind of problem from the one I described

The CPU framing was "the scan gets slower, so throughput decays". That is a degradation, and a session that is merely busy gets slower rather than broken. The memory framing is **unbounded**: there is no ceiling, no eviction, and no rate at which it becomes slow enough for anything to notice. A session that carries steady traffic accumulates without limit for as long as it stays up, and a long-lived router accumulates one such session per peer.

The CPU cost I measured (1.41 ms per datagram at a million packets) is the *symptom* that would eventually make it visible. The gigabyte is what happens if nothing intervenes first — and a router under memory pressure does not fail gracefully, it fails by being OOM-killed or by the BEAM giving up on the process.

For context on the rest of the tree, so the scale is legible: an established NTCP2 connection process is about 15 KB and **grows not at all** — `enter_data_phase/6` drops both the local keys and the remote RouterInfo after the handshake and retains only cipher state and two timer refs. This structure is the one place in a connection process where memory is proportional to elapsed time.

## What this changes for the ticket

Nothing in the acceptance criteria is wrong, and the bound still has to come from something the protocol already states rather than a round number. Two additions:

- [ ] The bound is justified on **memory** grounds, not only scan cost. A window wide enough to catch any legitimate resend is a small number of packets; the point is that it is small *and fixed*, and both reasons should be written down.
- [ ] A test that drives a long run of packets through a live session and asserts the process's memory does not grow past the bound. Asserting the *structure's* size is cheaper and sufficient; asserting process memory additionally catches anything else on the same state map that grows, which is the more valuable version of the test.

The diagnostic from that pass — that the set overtakes the entire rest of the connection process within one second of steady traffic at 1,000 packets/second — is the number worth keeping. It makes the case without arithmetic.

add.issue.name: An SSU2 session retains a RouterInfo it is not using, and NTCP2 does not

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

An SSU2 session that does not retain identity material it is not using, so the two transports stop disagreeing about what a connection process holds.

## The asymmetry, stated plainly

**NTCP2 does this correctly.** After the handshake, `enter_data_phase/6` hands `Local` and `RemoteRI` to the owner and calls `data_loop/6` with only the owner, the socket, the send cipher state, the receive stream, and two timer refs. A steady-state NTCP2 connection process holds no identity material at all. Measured at about 15 KB per connection and growing not at all.

**SSU2 retains the lot.** The session keeps its whole `config` map — including `local`, which carries our own RouterInfo and the Ed25519 signing seed — for the entire life of the session, and dereferences that nested map on every inbound datagram: the data path reads `maps:get(local, maps:get(config, State))` for the introduction key on four separate paths.

Measured, with a RouterInfo carrying both an NTCP2 and an SSU2 address: the RouterInfo term is **1,464 bytes**; the `local` map is **1,720 bytes**. At `max_ssu2_sessions = 32` that is **45.8 KB** of duplicated identity material held across sessions — small in absolute terms, but it scales linearly with the cap and it is duplication of a value that cannot change while a session is up.

## Why it is not simply "they forgot to drop it"

The retention is deliberate, and the comment at the boot wiring says so: the signing material and RouterInfo are carried "for the SSU2 peer-test Charlie/Bob roles (message 2 → 3 responder and introducer relay)". Someone thought about it and made a call.

**The capability that call serves is not currently reachable.** Both coordinators that would drive those roles — `i2p_peertest_coord` and `i2p_relay_coord` — have no child in the supervision tree, so nothing starts them and nothing in this retained material is ever read for the purpose it was retained for. Tracked on [7H7TSQR](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/7H7TSQR).

That makes this a **conditional** cost, and that is what makes it more than a tidiness ticket. Every SSU2 session pays for a role that no code currently performs.

## The decision this is really about

- **If the Charlie and peer-test roles ship**, the retention is justified and should stay — but the data path should still stop reaching three map levels deep for the introduction key on every packet, and the `out-of-session` paths that need the RouterInfo should be the only ones holding it.
- **If they do not ship yet**, the RouterInfo and signing seed should come out of the session's retained config now, and go back in when the coordinators are wired. The cost is then paid only by the sessions that can actually use it.
- **Either way**, what the steady-state data path needs from `local` is two keys: the introduction key and, for the Charlie path, the signing seed. It does not need a RouterInfo.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The steady-state data path reads what it needs without descending three map levels on every inbound datagram.
- [ ] A session's retained state is documented as what a data-phase session needs versus what a peer-test role needs, and the two are separable.
- [ ] If the peer-test roles remain unwired, the RouterInfo and signing seed are not retained by sessions that cannot use them. If they are wired, this ticket says so and the retention stays with a note explaining why.
- [ ] NTCP2 and SSU2 agree on this, and the answer says which one is right and why. Right now the correct behaviour exists in one transport and not the other, which is the same shape as the frame-decryption divergence on [DV3QSH3](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/DV3QSH3) — two transports written at different times, one of which has the better answer.
- [ ] A test asserts what a steady-state session retains, so a future field added to the local keys map does not silently become per-session retained state.

## Not in scope

The unbounded received-packet set, which is the larger memory problem on the same state map and is tracked on [7GP4A4K](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/7GP4A4K). At 16 bytes per packet received it reaches a gigabyte per session per day, which makes the 45.8 KB here a rounding error — but it is a different mechanism with a different fix, and folding the two together would obscure both.

Also checked and **not** a problem, so recorded here so nobody re-derives it: `out_pkts` is bounded after all. A resend timer is armed whenever the map is non-empty and empties it wholesale every 2 seconds regardless of what the peer does, so it is bounded by a timer rather than by the peer's cooperation. It looked unbounded on first reading and is not.

add.issue.comment.md:
## Solution: the receive set is now a bounded range list

**It was a flat list, prepended on every packet and never pruned** — one entry per packet for the life of the session, with a linear `lists:member/2` as the membership test. It is now a descending list of disjoint, non-adjacent inclusive `{Lo, Hi}` ranges, so a contiguous receive stream (what a healthy session actually sees) is a **single range** however long it runs. Memory is proportional to the number of *gaps* in the receive stream, not to its length.

**The bound is the ACK block's own reach, not a number I picked.** A block can only *name* a packet number within `?ACK_MAX + MaxRanges × 2 × ?ACK_MAX` of `AckThrough`. Nothing deeper can appear in any ACK the session sends, so retaining it cannot change one byte on the wire. That also bounds the pathological case, which is what makes it a real bound: a peer losing every other packet leaves at most `MaxRanges + 1` ranges, because that is how many a block can carry.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000,000 contiguous packets | ~16 MB, 1.6 ms/datagram | **1 range, 44 bytes** |
| every other packet lost | one entry per packet | **21 ranges, 284 bytes** |
| retained set, 20,000 packets | 20,000 numbers | **10,456 — the reach** |

### The part that was not obvious

Trimming the ranges is **not sufficient**, and the first version was wrong because of it. The numbers *between* the last retained range and the lowest number ever received were still never received, and the peer resends on a NACK — so that gap must be NACKed, not left unmentioned. A window keeping only its ranges falls silent there and strands a packet in the peer's resend map until the peer's own timer gives up.

So the lowest number ever received is carried **separately** from the ranges, and `build_ack/2`'s walk stops there. A session that received 3, 4, 5 and 1,000,000 retains only the last and still NACKs everything below it. Tested directly.

### The encoding is unchanged, and that was the risk worth the time

`build_ack/2` keeps its name and place in the codec but now walks the window. The concern was two implementations quietly disagreeing, so the rewrite was checked against the old list-based builder over **186,930 cases** — every range budget 0..30 crossed with 6,000 random receive sets and 31 fixed shapes — with **zero differences**, on both the untrimmed and the trimmed window. The spec's worked example, its literal wire bytes, and the round-trip all still pass, now driven *through* the window.

### The remaining checkbox: an out-of-window packet is visible

It cannot be recorded, so `add/3` reports `stale`, the session counts it in a new `ssu2_stale_packets` and logs `out_of_window`. Its blocks are still delivered — a real authenticated packet, and block handling is idempotent by message identity, so an unrecognised duplicate costs work rather than correctness. The spec requires retransmission to use a **fresh** number, so a peer doing this routinely is misbehaving and the counter says so.

## Two more defects, found while testing this and fixed in the same commit

**`become_established_common/3` never cleared `fragments` or `sr_info`.** It cleared every other data-phase field, so the handshake's inbound reassembly buffer stayed resident for the whole session, keeping the last SessionConfirmed fragment's payload alive. It was also why the session's heap depended on what the handshake happened to leave behind rather than on its data phase. (`sr_info` is written once and read nowhere, so dropping it is safe.)

**The e2e case needs its traffic chunked.** A 20,000-datagram burst overflows the listener socket, and with `data_resend_ms` parked for the case the dropped datagrams were never recovered — the wait simply never finished. Draining the receiver between chunks of 200 is backpressure rather than bookkeeping, and it is still a barrier: the receiver forwards only after decrypting and folding a packet into its window.

## On the memory assertion, which took three attempts

The follow-up called the process-memory version "the more valuable one". It is worth having, and it is also where I nearly shipped a flake — which the maintainer's standing rule against tolerances exists to prevent.

- **Comparing the session's total heap** flaked at 8,864 / 13,824 / 13,888 words with the window unchanged in every run. The difference was `remote_ri` (a RouterInfo a handshake leaves resident) and whatever the collector was holding. Comparing two such readings is a tolerance that has given up the ability to fail.
- **Comparing the window's byte size** was wrong more subtly: 41 → 44 bytes across the two rounds, which looks like growth and is not — 2,000 packets number to four digits and 20,000 to five, so the two boxed integers differ by a word. A size-in-bytes reading is exactly the kind of number that looks like a finding and is not one.
- **What is asserted now is the retained packet count**: 2,001 after 2,000 packets and 10,456 after 20,000. The window fills and then *stops*, and the ceiling is the reach. The heap is still bounded, but by a stated number rather than by comparison.

The two rounds are deliberately **not** compared for equality: they are supposed to differ, because a full window is the correct state and asserting they matched would assert that the window never fills.

## Gates

`just check` and `just dialyzer` pass. The e2e suite is clean over 5 consecutive repeats with identical readings. Dialyzer caught two real things on the way: an underspecified `new/0`, and a `contains/2` that rebuilt a window without `min_recv`, breaking its own contract.

## Not done, deliberately

`remote_ri` stays resident per session. It is read after establishment, so clearing it is a separate decision about what a session should hold rather than a side effect of this fix. Worth its own ticket if the accounting says sessions are numerous enough for 2 KB each to matter.

## Routing-path Tier 1: #7GP4A4K is built

The first of the three Tier 1 defects is done, in `c79feba`. **The SSU2 session's received-packet set no longer grows with traffic**, and the property is now structural rather than aspirational: the set is a list of ranges, so a contiguous receive stream is one entry for the life of the session.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000,000 contiguous packets | ~16 MB, 1.6 ms/datagram scan | 1 range, 44 bytes |

**The bound is the wire format's, not a tuning number**, which is what makes it defensible: an ACK block can only name a packet number within `255 + MaxRanges × 2 × 255` of `AckThrough`, so nothing deeper can appear in any ACK the session sends. add.issue.comment.md:
## Solved in `348df59`

All five checkboxes are met. **One wedged peer can no longer stop I2NP for any other peer**, and both halves are testable rather than asserted.

**The caller stopped waiting.** `i2p_ntcp2_conn:send/2` is a cast now — no `{send_done, Ref}` round trip, and the `{send, From, Ref, Payload}` shape is gone. That is the shape `i2p_ssu2_conn:send_i2np/4` already had, so the two transports are symmetric. The framing did **not** move to the caller and could not: the data phase is a stateful cipher stream, so the message number and SipHash IV must advance in the one process that owns them. What serialisation does not require is the *caller* waiting. That distinction is the change.

**The connection stopped blocking.** Casting alone would leave the process able to hang in `gen_tcp:send`, frames piling up behind it — a process that never returns is no better than one that blocks. So the data-phase socket is now `{delay_send, true}` with a `send_timeout`, turning the write into a question with a deadline. A peer that stops reading comes back `{error, timeout}` and the connection exits `{send_stalled, socket_blocked}`. **Only `delay_send` without a `send_timeout` is not a bound at all** — it waits for driver room indefinitely, the same unbounded wait one level down. Measured, OTP 28: 45 frames of 60 kB absorbed, the 46th times out; with a 4 kB `sndbuf`, 2 frames.

**Head-of-line, measured not assumed.** The ticket said a send "queues behind every inbound frame already buffered". On this tree that is **bounded at one inbound socket message** — the socket is `{active, once}` and re-armed only after the message in hand is processed, a structural invariant rather than a tuning number. Removing it entirely would mean two owners of one message number. The module doc says what the bound rests on.

**Two things found that the ticket did not name.** `stop/1` had the same unbounded wait (exported, documented to return `ok`, no `after` clause) — now bounded at 1 s. And `ntcp2_bytes_out` was charged *before* the write; it is now charged after, because refusing a frame is no longer a crash but a reachable outcome, and counting ahead would have counted bytes the router did not send.

### A defined outcome, on one instrument

New bus event `{peer_send_stalled, PeerHash, socket_blocked}`, with `socket_blocked()` an exported type. Per ADR 0002 it is **not** also logged, and the peer manager deliberately does **not** repeat the reason — it sees an ordinary disconnect and its backoff takes over. A test reading the reason from the manager would pass against a tree that had stopped announcing, so the test reads the bus. Added to ADR 0002's table as a seventh bus row, amendment noted.

### The tests — the first is the deliverable

- **`one_stalled_connection_does_not_stop_the_others`** — two peers, one healthy, one whose far end completed a real handshake then went silent. The manager's connection to the silent one is driven into a socket write, and a DatabaseLookup to the *healthy* peer still arrives.
- `a_peer_that_stops_reading_ends_the_connection` — the stall ends with the named reason and the bus event.
- `send_does_not_wait_on_the_connection` — a live pid that never drains its mailbox, and a dead pid. The dead-pid half is a second wait the old send had: it monitored nothing, so a connection that died between the caller's liveness check and its own message was a caller that never came back.
- `an_inbound_burst_does_not_delay_a_send` — the head-of-line bound: 10 probe frames through a 200-frame flood, order asserted.

**All four verified to fail against the old blocking send**, not assumed to: the conn case hits `timetrap_timeout`, the manager case times out waiting for the healthy frame.

add.issue.comment.md:
### Two harness findings worth carrying

**`erlang:suspend_process/1` is unusable in this tree.** The obvious way to make a peer stop reading is to suspend the connection process that owns the socket. It deadlocks the node's **code server** as soon as the suspended process is anywhere near a module load — I watched the peer manager itself wedge in `code_server:call` with the code server `waiting`, and take the suite's other connections down with it. `sys:suspend/1` is worse: a connection is a plain receive loop and answers no system messages, so the call simply times out. Neither is recoverable mid-suite.

The replacement is `i2p_ct_helpers:silent_ntcp2_peer/1`: it completes a real NTCP2 responder handshake with the library's own stream readers, then never reads its socket again. About thirty lines, suspends nothing, and leaves nothing behind for a later case to trip over. The peer announces itself when it has parked, which is also the barrier the case needs — waiting on a timer instead would race the handshake, since frames sent before the peer parks get drained and the socket never fills.

**One of the tests was nearly a false pass.** The manager flushes queued lookups on connect, so a DatabaseLookup was already sitting in the test mailbox from before the stall began. "Wait for a lookup" was therefore satisfiable by that stale frame whether or not the manager could still reach anybody — true in exactly the situation the case exists to detect is fixed. It now drains the mailbox first and looks up a key minted after the drain, so the frame it waits for is provably its own. Worth naming because the version that passed for the wrong reason would have kept passing after a regression.

A third, smaller one: the RouterInfo hash covers the *identity*, not the published addresses, so two RouterInfos built from the same router are the same peer with two ports. The case needs three distinct routers, not two.

### Verification

`just check` and `just dialyzer` both clean — **850 eunit, 215 CT**. The two touched suites repeated 3x with no flakes. `erlfmt` clean.

### Left standing

Nothing blocked. **#ZYQ227K** — the NTCP2 listener accepting one inbound connection per second — is the remaining Tier 1 item and is untouched by this.
