add.issue.name: The SAM listener accepts one inbound session per second

edit.description.md:
Found while fixing #ZYQ227K, which is this same code. Not measured separately: the loop is character-for-character the NTCP2 one, so the measured rate carries over.

## The defect

`i2p_sam_listener` is a hand-rolled `proc_lib` accept loop that waits on its control messages (`port`, `address`, `stop`) on a **1-second receive timeout**, and calls `gen_tcp:accept` only when that timeout expires. At most one inbound SAM session per second, unconditionally — the same "the rate is exactly the timeout, not a load effect" finding #ZYQ227K recorded for NTCP2.

## Why it is worth more here than it was on NTCP2

SAM is how a client reaches the router. An I2P application opens a connection per session, and a client that reconnects — or opens a second session while the first is still being set up — waits a second for each. `i2p_sam_sup` starts this as a **boot listener**, so it is on the default path of every router with SAM on, not behind an option.

## Do

- [ ] Accept is no longer rate-limited by the control-message poll. The measurement behind #ZYQ227K's fix applies here unchanged: a listening socket delivers no message when a connection arrives, whatever its `{active, _}` (verified at OTP 28, written up in `m:i2p_ntcp2_acceptor`'s module doc), so a process that accepts either blocks in `gen_tcp:accept` with nothing else to do or polls it on a timer.
- [ ] **Reuse `m:i2p_ntcp2_acceptor` or write a SAM one — decide, and say why.** This is the only real question. The acceptor as written is NTCP2-specific: it builds a `role => bob` connection child and hands the socket to an NTCP2 handshake. A shared accept loop parameterised by a "start this session with this socket" fun would serve both, at the cost of a fun crossing the process boundary once per connection; two acceptors cost a second copy of the loop. Either is defensible; the ticket is worth doing deliberately rather than by copying.
- [ ] A test that opens a batch of inbound connections and asserts they are accepted within a stated bound — the bound asserted, not a sleep. `apps/i2per/test/i2p_sam_SUITE.erl` has the fixtures.
- [ ] The handover invariant is stated next to the handover. The accepted socket inherits its listen socket's active mode, so `{active, false}` on the listen socket is what makes the window between `accept` and `controlling_process/2` harmless; the session's `{socket_ready, Sock}` ordering rests on the same fact and currently has no comment saying so.

## Deliberately not a third ticket

`i2p_sam_proxy` also accepts on a 1-second timeout, but only `apps/i2per/test/i2p_sam_SUITE.erl` starts it — it is test scaffolding that ships in `src/`, which #EK2KTKP already tracks. It rides on that ticket rather than getting one of its own.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: the accept moved to `m:i2p_ntcp2_acceptor`, a process per listener whose whole job is to block in `f:gen_tcp:accept/1`. Commit `e14b5177`. A burst of six inbound connections now drains in **under a millisecond**, against 6.06 s before.

**A listening socket cannot notify**, which is what forced the poll. Verified on this tree at OTP 28: with `{active, true}`, `{active, once}` and `{active, false}` it delivers **no message of any kind** when a connection arrives, and `inet_drv.c` arms `FD_ACCEPT` in exactly one place — `INET_REQ_ACCEPT`, while a `gen_tcp:accept` call is outstanding. So a process that accepts has two options: block in `accept` and answer nothing while it does, or come out of it on a timer to check its mailbox. The old loop took the second with a 1 s timeout and paid at exactly the timeout's rate. Both options still exist, so the fix is a process rather than a trick.

**The handover is unchanged and now says what it rests on.** An accepted socket **inherits its listen socket's active mode** — measured, not assumed: the same accept over an active listener yields a socket that delivers `{tcp, Sock, Data}` to the acceptor, over a passive one it does not. That is why the listen socket is passive, and why the accepted socket is set passive again at the one process that owns it between `accept` and `controlling_process/2`: a socket that cannot deliver cannot deliver to the wrong owner, so the invariant holds by construction rather than by the loop being quick.

**The control messages now have a process that is not blocked** to answer them, which is what the timeout existed for. The loop has no timeout clause at all.

## Two things beyond the four checkboxes, both found on the way

- **`port/1` and `address/1` waited for their answer with no bound** — a caller whose listener was not there never came back, the same class as the previous ticket's `stop/1`. The bound moved to the caller's end, since the loop no longer has a timeout to serve: they raise `{listener_unanswered, _, _}` after `?CONTROL_TIMEOUT_MS`, and `stop/1` kills a listener that does not answer, as `f:i2p_ntcp2_conn:stop/1` does. A dead listener is a fast answer because of the monitor, not the timeout.
- **An accept error other than `closed` exited as a `case_clause`**, naming nothing. Now `{accept_failed, Reason}`, and the listener ends with the acceptor, so a live listener pid can never be a port that has quietly stopped accepting while `port/1` still reports it.

## One thing deliberately not done

A connection the limit refuses is closed silently, as before. I wrote a `i2p_log:debug/2` frame for it and **the gate refused it**: `i2p_log_tests` exists to hold the set of frame-emitting modules at four, and a fifth means the fold it certifies is unfinished. That test is right and my frame was a nicety, so it went. An event has nowhere to key either — the handshake has not run, so there is no peer hash — so this is recorded here rather than instrumented.

### The test, and how it was checked

`a_batch_of_inbound_connections_is_not_accepted_one_per_second`. Six **real** NTCP2 dials fired at the same instant, each in its own process — a sequential loop would measure the accept rate with a peer already established between each pair, which is not the condition the defect was measured under.

Both sides of every accept are counted. `dialed` is `f:i2p_ntcp2_conn:connect/3` returning, so the accept let the dialer through; `accepted` is the responder announcing to this process as the listener's owner, and a Bob process exists only because its socket was accepted. All twelve must land inside **one 2 s budget**, which is a batch bound: against the defect the floor is (N-1) = 5 s, so a regression that admitted five immediately and the sixth a second later fails on the sixth rather than passing on the five that were fast.

**Verified it fails that way**, by putting `timer:sleep(1000)` back in the accept loop:

```
{accept_batch_incomplete,[{dialed,[<0.572.0>]},{accepted,[<0.578.0>]}]}
```

The case also pins the second checkbox, which is the easy one to lose while fixing the throttle: a separate process asks the listener for its port while the batch is in flight and must get the right answer. It cannot pass slowly — `port/1` is bounded, so a control path stuck behind an accept raises rather than returning. A second assertion covers the bound from the other end, against a listener that is gone.

**One trap recorded in the case itself:** Common Test reads a case that *returns* `{'EXIT', Reason}` as a case that failed with `Reason`. An assertion helper that catches into `{'EXIT', {Reason, Stack}}` therefore fails the case **even when its match succeeded** — which is what happened here for longer than it should have, since the failure text is the error the assertion was about. The case ends `ok` and says why.

### Gates

`erlfmt` clean, `dialyzer` clean, **850 eunit + 216 CT pass**. The conn suite three times over, the peer-transport and boot suites twice, no flakes.

### Next

Filed [#EP6SRK1](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/EP6SRK1) for what this turned up: **`i2p_sam_listener` is this same loop**, character for character, with the session spawn swapped in — one inbound SAM session per second, on a listener `i2p_sam_sup` starts at boot. edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## Question

How much of the work in front of an SSU2 connection is actually that connection's, and how much is every connection's?

The answer today: the shared listener does a lot of it. There is one listener process per bound address, it owns the only UDP socket, and on the way in and out of every datagram it does work that belongs to one session.

## What it does that belongs to a session

**Classification repeats itself.** Resolving a datagram's owner runs the long-header unmask up to three times: once in the initial classification, once when no session or pending endpoint claimed it, and once more in the handshake fallback. Each unmask is three raw ChaCha20 passes and two XORs.

**Measured, per 1472-byte datagram:** one long-header unmask is **2.38 µs**. A full AEAD decrypt of the same datagram — the actual work the session exists to do — is **1.40 µs**. So the shared listener spends roughly five times the crypto of the real work before handing the datagram to the process that will actually process it.

**The Charlie role runs inline.** Responding as Charlie to an out-of-session peer test is a role, and a per-connection one: decode the probe, build the reply, AEAD-encode it, send it. It executes in the listener, not in a connection process, because at that point there is no session to own it.

**The send path is centralised by necessity.** Only the listener can send, since it alone holds the socket, so every outbound datagram for every session is a cast into this one process — plus a byte count and up to four debug frames.

## Do

Preserve what the module doc argues for and change what it does. The routing order in that doc is a correctness fix, not a preference: reading the type byte first diverts roughly one SessionCreated in 256 into the Charlie responder, which drops it, and the peer dies with a handshake timeout an average of once every few thousand handshakes. Any simplification that reintroduces a type-byte-first decision undoes a bug that was expensive to find.

- [x] Classification does the minimum crypto that is still exact, and the number of unmask passes per datagram is stated and justified in the module doc.
- [x] The Charlie responder is either a per-connection process or a worker that cannot hold up datagram classification, and the answer says which and why.
- [x] The measured per-datagram cost in the socket owner drops, and the measurement is recorded in the ticket so the improvement is checkable rather than asserted.
- [x] The one-in-256 SessionCreated regression has a test.

| | passes | µs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `i2p_ssu2:open_conn_id/3` — routing | 1 | 0.76 |
| `i2p_ssu2:open_header16/3` — the type byte | 2 | 1.55 |
| `i2p_ssu2:open_long/3` — what routing used to cost | 3 | 2.30 |
| AEAD decrypt of the body, which the session then runs | (1) | 1.40 |
| answering one out-of-session probe, Charlie role | 8 | 6.80 |

So the socket owner, per datagram:

| the datagram is... | passes | µs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| claimed by a session or a pending dialer | **1** | 0.76 |
| from an unknown endpoint: probe, SessionRequest, or junk | 3 | 1.55 |
| from an unknown endpoint: TokenRequest | 5 | 4.80 |

**2.30 µs → 0.76 µs** on the hot path, against 1.40 µs for the decrypt it exists to enable.

## The approach

Two new functions in `i2p_ssu2`, and the listener uses nothing else:

- `open_conn_id/3` — bytes 0..7 only. The destination connection id is what both lookups key on, and nothing else is worth opening until a lookup has failed. One pass.
- `open_header16/3` — bytes 0..15, two passes, no third: bytes 16..31 stay encrypted. Only meaningful for a datagram addressed to our own introduction key out of session, which is the only place the listener reads a type byte.

The classification then stops at the first answer that can be true. **One open for the unowned path, not three:** PeerTest, SessionRequest and TokenRequest are disjoint type bytes, so testing order is immaterial and the single `open_header16/3` answers all three. `decode_token_request/2` is the only call left that re-opens, and only a datagram whose type byte already says TokenRequest reaches it — that one legitimately pays, because the decision needs the blocks. Junk went from nine passes to three.

## The Charlie role

`i2p_ssu2_charlie`: one `temporary` worker per listener, a cast in and a cast out, so a busy, wedged or dead responder cannot delay classification. Started on first use rather than in `init/1` — a listener asking its own supervisor for a child from `init/1` re-enters the supervisor that is starting that listener, and deadlocks. Also the cheaper shape: a router never tested as Charlie never starts one. It sits outside `session_limit/0` deliberately; that limit exists to bound Noise handshake state and a responder holds one public key.

The listener monitors it, so its death costs the role and not the send path every session shares, and a failed replacement resets the pid to `undefined` so the next probe tries again rather than casting at a corpse forever.

## What is checked, not asserted

`classification_spends_one_pass_per_claimed_datagram` counts `i2p_crypto:chacha20_crypt/4` calls in the listener process — the primitive every unmask pass ends at, so the count is passes. Reverting the hot path to `open_long/3` makes it report 3 and 5 and fail; I checked.

Two notes for whoever reads the diff:

- the trace pattern needs `[local]`, or it silently counts zero on same-module calls. The case that first tried to measure this reported 0 for exactly that reason.
- the module's `i2p_log:debug` site count is unchanged at 14: three left with the Charlie role, three arrived with the role's new plumbing, and the two sites the handshake fallback lost collapsed into one `drop` frame shared by both of its ways of failing.

Routing order is unchanged and still session → pending → type byte, so the one-in-256 `SessionCreated` still cannot be diverted into the responder; `created_with_peertest_type_byte_is_delivered` covers it and `i2p_ssu2_peertest_SUITE` covers the role end to end through the new process.

Full gate green: 218 CT, 851 eunit, erlfmt, dialyzer, docs.

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

A Common Test run should not spend three quarters of its wall clock starting and stopping applications.

Found while resolving #T3WH4EM, which named three costs and this is not one of them. It is the biggest one.

## Measured

Full 25-suite run at working-copy parent `ed2e0642`, `rebar3 ct --sname i2per_ct`:

- **545 s wall**, 218 cases.
- **123.9 s** of that is inside case bodies. The remaining **~420 s, about 77%, is outside every case.**
- Suite setup is not the cost. All 48 `init_per_suite`/`end_per_suite` entries report `=elapsed 0.0s`.
- 222 cases pay it individually, so ~1.9 s each of setup and teardown.

## Where it goes

Per-testcase lifecycle, repeated per case rather than per suite:

- `application:ensure_all_started/1` and `application:stop/1`, in `start_app/2` and `teardown/0` across the SSU2, NTCP2, SAM, peer, netdb, tunnel and boot suites
- the SSU2 frame trace start/stop in `i2p_ct_helpers`, which installs and removes a `logger` handler each time
- per-case app env set/unset pairs, which are cheap individually and are not the cost
- `create_priv_dir, auto_per_tc`, which creates a fresh priv dir per case

## Why it matters

This is not the ticket's "the test suite is slow" problem, and treating it as one would mean rewriting suites that are already fine. The distribution is concentrated: **16 cases at 2 s or more carry 73% of the 123.9 s of case time**, and 234 entries finish under a second. Those two facts together mean the cases are cheap and the scaffolding around them is not.

So the cost is per-case fixed overhead multiplied by case count, which is the shape that grows worst when a suite is split into more cases for clarity. Every future case pays ~1.9 s whether it asserts anything interesting or not.

## The question to answer first

**What is a case's lifetime supposed to be?** The suites mostly tear the application down between cases because it is the only way to guarantee a clean `i2p_events` handler set, a fresh NetDb, and no inherited app env. That isolation is real and several cases depend on it. The question is which of those genuinely need application-level isolation and which only need their own state, because a per-case `i2p_config` reset or a per-case fixture directory would serve the second group without stopping the VM's application controller each time.

That is a decision to make, not a change to make: the right answer might be "leave it, and accept a nine-minute gate", which is legitimate if the isolation is worth more than the time. But the current state is a nine-minute gate that nobody chose, which is the thing worth fixing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The per-case cost is attributed before anything is changed: how much is `ensure_all_started`/`stop`, how much is the trace handler, how much is the priv dir. Measured, not estimated.
- [ ] Which cases genuinely need application restart is stated, and the rest get the cheaper isolation that is actually equivalent for what they assert.
- [ ] A case that does not need the application restarted costs materially less than one that does.
- [ ] The isolation the restart provides is not weakened. Any case relying on a clean handler set, a fresh NetDb, or unset app env keeps it.
- [ ] Wall and case time are re-measured and both recorded, since "faster" and "the cases still mean something" have to be shown together.
- [ ] The answer says whether `create_priv_dir` should stay `auto_per_tc`, which is a per-case filesystem cost that is not free either.

## Not in scope

The 16 genuinely heavy cases. `receive_window_does_not_grow_with_traffic` pushes 22,000 real datagrams through a live session in 19 s and is doing its job; the `i2p_peer_transport` cluster is protocol-mandated timeout and backoff and overlaps #HXT1P2D. Neither is scaffolding, and making either faster would mean asserting less.

Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## Resolved

Implemented and measured. See the two resolution comments for the before/after table, the code, and the demonstration.

**Read the criteria below as amended.** The decision taken while resolving this (delete the duplicate rather than police it) made two of them moot and one of them actively misleading, and they are amended here so a reader who only has the body is not sent to build a test that was deliberately not built.

## What was built

**A unit-test run that is quick enough to run often**, and a gate that cannot silently stop running a suite.

## Measured

**EUnit: 12.94 s → 9.21 s, 851 tests.** The single 5.022 s case is now 0.033 s.

**CT: 545 s → 510 s.** Barely moved, and the reason is not in this ticket: ~420 s of the run is per-testcase application start and stop, which is now [#WA1R7SY](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/WA1R7SY).

The distribution claim below reproduces and is sharper than stated: **16 cases at 2 s or more carry 73%** of the 123.9 s spent inside case bodies. The absolute figures did not reproduce on the measuring machine (545 s against 2 m 19 s).

## The three items, and what happened to each

### 1. One test was 36% of the EUnit run, and the cost was a hardcoded constant — DONE

`derived_figures_appear_after_two_readings` took 5.022 s because it needs two readings and `?POLL_MS = 5000` was hardcoded. `i2per_status_state` now reads `poll_ms` on the pattern already in `i2p_netdb_srv`, shipped default unchanged at 5000, and the test sets it to 20 ms. It now costs 0.033 s with the same assertion and no dependence on poll alignment.

The diagnosis was right. The interval is also the window the derived figures are differenced over, so it is now documented as the resolution of every rate on the page rather than as a tuning knob.

### 2. Two RSA-4096 keys per test run — DONE, but not the way this ticket said

**The original text of this item was wrong and is withdrawn.** It said 4096 was over-specified and to drop to 2048. `i2p_su3` accepts nothing else: the decoder rejects any signature type but `16#0006` and any length but 512 bytes, which is a 4096-bit modulus. A smaller key produces a container the router itself declares malformed.

The original count was also wrong: there are four memoised 4096-bit keygen sites, and an EUnit run pays for **three** of them, not two.

What shipped is the duplicate-generation fix: `i2p_ct_helpers:su3_keypair/0` and `su3_other_keypair/0`, generated once per run, called from all four sites. EUnit 3 keygens to 2, CT 2 to 1. Three of the four were also generating a certificate under a different subject name for the same key.

### 3. Nothing enforces that the suite list matches the suites on disk — DONE, by deleting the list

This is the item whose shape changed. The list in `rebar.config` was a hand-maintained copy of the set of suites on disk, which is what the project's standing preference forbids: one place is the source and the other refers to it.

So the list is gone. rebar3 auto-discovers every `*_SUITE.erl` under an app's `test/`, and the i2pd interop suite moved to `apps/i2per/interop/`, a directory rebar3 does not discover, so its exclusion from `just check` is structural. A suite added to disk now runs, with no config edit.

The silent failure was confirmed real before changing anything: `rebar3 help ct` shows `--abort_if_missing_suites` defaulting to true, which catches a suite that is *listed but absent*, and there is no option for the reverse.

## Acceptance criteria, as amended

- [x] The poll interval is injectable, following the pattern already in `i2p_netdb_srv`, with the shipped default unchanged.
- [x] No test **generates a duplicate** signing key, and the reason the key is 4096 bits is written at the keygen. *(Amended. The original read "no test generates a key larger than the property under test needs", which reads as licence to shrink the one key that cannot be shrunk.)*
- [x] A suite file added to `test/` runs without any config change. *(Amended. The original asked for a test asserting `rebar.config` and the test directory agree, which describes a test that watches a duplicate. There is no duplicate to watch. Demonstrated, not asserted: a throwaway `probe_gate_SUITE` was dropped into `test/`, the full gate ran it with no config edit, and it passed.)*
- [x] EUnit and CT wall times re-measured, before and after recorded in the resolution comments.

## What is not in question

The test infrastructure is good and was not touched. Only 19 `timer:sleep` calls exist across 75 test files and the ones that do are principled. `i2p_ct_helpers:events_from/1` barriers on a known event announced after the work, precisely because a notify call returning is not a delivery guarantee, and accumulates rather than discards so negative assertions work. `no_timer_is_scheduled_test` observes with a trace rather than waiting and hoping. `catch` never wraps an assertion anywhere, and 38 files use `try...after` for cleanup.

Do not "fix" any of that.

## Found on the way, and filed elsewhere

**[#WA1R7SY](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/WA1R7SY) — per-testcase application start and stop is the largest block of CT wall time.** ~420 s of a 545 s run, outside every case body, repeated across 222 cases at roughly 1.9 s each. It is bigger than all three costs on this ticket combined, and it was not on the list.

## Destination

**i2per 0.2.0: a release an operator who did not write it can run, and see.**

Two claims, and the point of this release is that **both are checkable using the things 0.2.0 itself ships**:

1. *We ship a versioned, public read API over the router's state.* Cumulative byte counters at the transport boundary **and** the transit relay, uptime, tunnel-build outcomes, and a documented additive-only contract, with `i2p_stats` as the counter home inside the core. The core supplies data; a presentation app aggregates.
2. *We ship a logging floor.* All eight standard levels with a written discipline, `notice` as the default, a hot `log_level` key, a configurable formatter, and a 3am checklist of what must be recorded for a fault to be diagnosable without reading the source.

Plus the boundaries that keep both sustainable: the core is data-only and never renders ([ADR 0001](https://github.com/freke/i2per/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-data-only-core-with-presentation-apps.md)), and deployment is a separate repository.

**What 0.2.0 deliberately does not do: change network behaviour.**

Being a Charlie and measuring reachability — the two claims this map originally targeted — move to **0.3.0**. The reasoning is verification, not size. Those are protocol claims, and their only oracle is the i2pd interop suite, which does not run in CI. Telemetry and logging let you *debug* a protocol claim; they cannot *verify* it. So the two groups have different verification stories, and the observability release is the one whose claims are self-verifying. Building it first is what makes 0.3.0 provable rather than merely done.

The decisions on those two tickets already stand and are not reopened by this re-draw. Only their release assignment moves.
## Notes

**Domain:** an Erlang/OTP I2P router (`apps/i2per`) plus a standalone status web service (`apps/i2per_status`). `i2per` is the model provider, not a person.

**Vocabulary** — the I2P spec's, not i2pd's. This map pins down three terms the tree currently uses loosely:

- **Charlie** — the router an *Alice* asks to introduce it to a *Bob*. i2per is currently an Alice only. "Being a Charlie" is the 0.2.0 claim.
- **Measured reachability** — reachability established by an actual peer test, as opposed to the current config echo.
- **Network credibility** — how the live network treats i2per: whether peers can intros it, and whether it can intros them.
- **Core** — the `i2per` application itself: transports, tunnels, NetDb, SAM. It exposes state through Erlang APIs only, and **never** has a GUI or TUI and never serves HTTP.
- **Presentation app** — a separate OTP application that connects to a core node over Erlang distribution and supplies a GUI, TUI, or external API for others to consume. `i2per_status` is the first. Both same-node and separate-node operation are supported.

**Release roadmap** (maintainer's): **0.1.0 is not finished yet** — the repo's 0.1.0 is still a development snapshot, not a published release. **0.2.0** is the destination of this map. **1.0.0 is a full match to i2pd as it is today**, still excluding the legacy protocols. So the i2pd-parity items — tunnel build v2, Charlie selection, congestion control and RTT, hole-punch Half B, LeaseSet v1, SOCKS/HTTP proxy/BOB/I2PControl, TUN, console CLI — are 1.0.0 material, and the map's two scope tickets should resolve that way rather than by re-litigating it.

**Owned elsewhere, deliberately not ticketed here.** 0.1.0's identity is "we can connect to the I2P network without causing harm", and the maintainer has folded making that claim explicit and tested into **finishing 0.1.0 directly**. It is not on this board and should not be re-filed here. Worth knowing why it is not a trivial claim: the property already holds (the shipped profile bounds transit and disables live participation, and `i2per_sup:validate_host/1` refuses a non-public published host unless `allow_private_host` is set), but nothing tests it — which means a future change could quietly break the one property the release is named for.

**Standing preferences:**

- **A test that can flake is a design or test defect, not bad luck.** The
  maintainer's rule, added 2026-09-28 after three flakes in one session were
  investigated: in Erlang a test can be made deterministic, so a non-deterministic
  test means something has not been synchronised on. The distinctions that matter:
  a **barrier** is a received message, a monitor, or a `gen_server:call` issued
  after the event — all of which are ordered by the runtime and cannot race; a
  **deadline** is a hope, and a **tolerance** is a flake with extra steps that has
  also given up the ability to fail. Polling a state predicate until a deadline is
  a barrier in disguise and is treated as one. So is a `timer:sleep` whose
  guarantee is asserted (`Uptime >= 1500` after sleeping 1500) — that cannot fail
  on a fast machine, unlike a sleep that hopes some work has finished. A property
  that cannot be tested without moving the system clock, or a hostile scheduler,
  is documented as untested rather than covered by a case that re-asserts
  something adjacent under a misleading name.
- **Data should never be duplicated.** If two places must agree about a value, one of them is the source and the other refers to it — never two hand-maintained copies. This is why the read API's key set is a single exported list, and it generalises to any contract a consumer depends on.


- **Legacy is out**, by the maintainer's call: NTCP1, SSU1, I2CP, ElGamal/DSA, Datagram1. The release profile already refuses them.
- **Instrumentation lands with the behaviour.** A ticket that touches a path adds its counters and events there. Nothing is deferred to a later ticket.
- **Gates:** `rebar.config` compiles with `warnings_as_errors`. `just check` and `just dialyzer` are release gates. The i2pd interop suite is *not* currently in `ct_opts`.
- **Both statuses are allowed:** `i2per_status` may run on the router's own node (needs no distribution, since `router_node` already defaults to `node()`) or on a separate node the operator connects. The map must not collapse this into one option.

**Every session consults:** `erlang`, `domain-modeling`, and `wayfinder`.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket, enough to judge relevance, then zoom the link -->

- [The 0.2.0 telemetry contract: counters, events, uptime](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/3H11881): a new `i2p_stats` gen_server in the core owns `counters` refs behind a public, versioned read API; bytes are counted at the transport boundary **and** the transit relay (six points); the core supplies cumulative data and the client aggregates, which is what keeps `i2p_stats` timer-free; four new events land on already-touched paths. Also settled here: the core never renders, and deployment is another repo.
- [What does i2pd's HTTP status monitor show, field for field?](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/1KJMFBH): i2pd's monitor is 22 main-page fields plus 10 detail pages (and **no graph page and no XMLRPC** — don't chase them). i2per already surfaces 7 and *holds* ~25 more, so most of it is accessor work — including the entire LeaseSets panel, the single biggest cheap win. Every **derived** value, by contrast, is new state: uptime, all six bandwidth rates, both tunnel-success ratios. Byte counting is the keystone, and no module in the tree counts a byte today.
- [What does the network require of a Charlie, and what breaks without it?](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/K84PJ0N): The role splits cleanly — an in-session half (verify RelayIntro, answer with a signed **reject**) that alone removes the real harm and needs no new crypto, plus an optional out-of-session HolePunch datagram that is not 0.2.0's problem. Nobody selects a Charlie they lack an established *outgoing* session with, so this work sequences **after** reachability, not beside it. The gap survived 0.1.0 because the protocol has no introduction-failed signal at all.

- [Three test-suite costs, and one silent coverage gap](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/T3WH4EM): EUnit 12.94 s → 9.21 s. The status poll interval becomes `poll_ms`, documented as the window the derived rates are differenced over rather than a tuning knob; the four duplicate RSA-4096 test keygens become one shared identity per run (4096 itself is fixed — `i2p_su3` accepts nothing but a 512-byte signature); and the `ct_opts` suite list is **deleted rather than policed**, so a suite on disk cannot be forgotten and the interop suite is excluded by living outside `test/`. Also settled: the biggest cost in the gate is neither of these — ~420 s of a 545 s CT run is per-testcase application start and stop ([#WA1R7SY](https://github.com/freke/i2per/issues/WA1R7SY)).
## Not yet specified

- **Open design decisions in the status page itself** — now that the field inventory exists, these are sharp but belong past 0.2.0's two claims: does the page report *absent* services (five of i2pd's six have no i2per feature behind them) or omit them; and does i2per gain a per-tunnel state, given it splits pools into maps and "failed" is currently transient, or does a parity page render pool membership under a different name?
- **Operator surface beyond SAM and the status page** — SOCKS, HTTP proxy, I2PControl/BOB, an interactive console. Undecided, and it interacts with the TUN question.
- **TUN interface** — whether transparent IP-in/IP-out is ever in scope, and what it costs once a SOCKS proxy exists.
- **Event-schema versioning on the cross-node bus** — `i2p_events_forward` has no negotiation, so a router upgrade can silently break a remote subscriber. Real, but not urgent until a second consumer exists.
- **Packaging beyond relx** — deb, static binary, container. 0.2.0 ships the relx tarball; whether that is the right operator artifact is open.
- **0.3.0's shape beyond the two decided tickets** — peer test first, then the Charlie role, then reachability-aware hop selection. The first two are internally sequenced and worth treating as one piece of work. Beyond them: congestion control and RTT estimation, which is where the byte counters from 0.2.0 finally get a consumer.
- **Datagram2 replay protection** — a correctness gap in `i2p_datagram.erl`, not a feature. It fits no pillar and goes unnoticed until someone is replayed at.
- **Addressbook publication** — i2per subscribes to remote addressbooks but never publishes its own `hosts.txt`.
- **Hole punching as a Charlie** — the out-of-session half (HolePunch type 11 to the endpoint Alice signed, then a responder session). Separable from 0.2.0's in-session half, and sharp enough to ticket once that lands. **Carry the spec defect forward:** the Hole Punch section specifies `type :: 7`, but 7 is PeerTest and i2pd uses 11 — implementing the text literally routes a punch into the receiver's peer-test handler.
- **Spec diagram drift, generally** — the SSU2 spec's *diagrams* contradict its own section headings and message table (Hole Punch diagram says 7, heading and table say 11; Peer Test diagram says 10 inside a Type 7 section; Token Request says 6 inside a Type 10 section). The rule established: **read the heading, never the diagram.** Worth a note in `docs/protocol.md` when the Charlie work lands.
- **Live interop against a Java peer** — the Java Charlie findings are source-level only; i2p-java 0.9.70 at `bb530daa` was read but never built or run. A real interop run is the only way to confirm, and the canonical source mirror is `github.com/i2p/i2p.i2p` (`.i2p` is an I2P-only pseudo-TLD and NXDOMAIN off-net).

- **Path migration in SSU2.** Past the destination; blocks 18/19 stay keepalive-echo.

## Fork resolved: ETS table + paired `gb_trees`, decided with the maintainer

The existence check is now a table read. Measured, not asserted:

```
trivial gen_server:call floor : 1.325 us
i2p_netdb_srv:find/1 (miss)  : 1.266 us      <- was, per frame, on the relay path
ets:member/2  (no copy)      : 0.1047 us
ets:lookup/2   (copies RI)   : 0.3060 us
```

Roughly **12x** off the per-frame path, and the answer no longer copies a RouterInfo. The lookup cost *nothing* above a bare call to an empty `gen_server`, which is what the ticket's 1.39 us against a 1.28 us floor already implied.

Verified as properties, not hoped for: a non-owner `ets:insert` raises `badarg`, so **single-writer is enforced by ETS rather than by convention**; and the table dies with its owner, so the NetDb cannot outlive its process.

### The order is a value, not a table

`Seq -> Hash` and `Hash -> Seq`, both `gb_trees`, both inside the store map. Only the routers went to ETS, because only they need concurrent read. If the order were a second table it would be side-effect state and the module's central property — one function between every mutation and both structures — would be lost.

**`queue` was the obvious candidate and is the wrong shape.** Its O(1) removals (`out/1`, `drop/1`, `out_r/1`, `drop_r/1`) reach only the two ends; promoting a router to most-recent is a delete from the middle, which is `delete/2` and O(n). At the shipped capacity of 5000:

| operation | list (was) | queue | paired gb_trees |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| promote to MRU | 17.30 us | ~17 us (O(n)) | **2.09 us** |
| evict LRU | 19.93 us | **O(1)** | 0.07 us |
| capacity check | 6.87 us | O(1) | 0.02 us |

Queue would have sped up the cold path and left the hot one exactly as slow.

A single `gb_trees` keyed by `{Seq, Hash}` was tried first and is a **dead end**: eviction is 0.07 us, but promoting is impossible, because deleting needs the `{Seq, Hash}` key and a caller holding only a hash cannot form it. `gb_trees` has keyed lookup only, no remove-by-value. Hence the pair.

### Criterion 3: one authority for the existence question

`ets:member` reading one table cannot disagree with itself. `i2p_netdb_srv:has_router/1` is the only function that answers "do we hold this RouterInfo" and it answers from the table alone.

The order is a second structure and it *could* drift, so `i2p_netdb:self_check/1` is a real function: it asserts the table and the order hold the same count, that every hash in each is in the other, and that `order_pos` is exactly the inverse of `order`. The maintenance preference on this project is that data is never duplicated — so where a second structure exists it is checked in the one place that can see both, rather than assumed correct.

### Criterion 5: the drop is counted

New counter `transit_frames_dropped_no_route`. It answers "why is my inbound figure not equal to my outbound figure", which the two byte counters cannot answer between them. A counter rather than an event, because a transit hop whose next hop has expired is a steady state and an event per 1028-byte frame would drown the bus.

### Both call sites

`send_tunnel_data/2` (per frame, the hot one) and `forward_stb/4` (per build record). The second is not hot and there is no reason to pay for a RouterInfo nobody reads.

### Progress

`i2p_netdb` is rewritten and its 38 unit tests pass unmodified except one round-trip assertion that compared stores by identity, which cannot hold now that a store carries a tid. Full EUnit: **851 passed**. Not yet run: dialyzer, CT, and the full gate.

## A sharp edge in the deletion, found the hard way

Twice now a stale copy under `_build/test/lib/i2per/test/` has failed the gate with a message naming the *wrong* suite:

```
%%% i2p_tunnel_srv_exploratory_SUITE ==> error_in_suite: FAILED
%%% i2p_tunnel_srv_exploratory_SUITE ==> 'probe_gate_SUITE cannot be compiled or loaded'
```

rebar3 copies the test sources into `_build` and does not prune the copies of files that have since been deleted. Auto-discovery reads that directory, so a deleted `*_SUITE.erl` is picked up, fails to compile, and is reported against whichever suite happened to be running.

This is a real cost of removing the list, and it is worth naming rather than remembering: **under a suite list a stale copy was harmless, because nothing consulted the directory.** The trade is that this failure is loud and names the right fix, where the old one was silent and named nothing.

`rebar3 clean` clears it. Worth saying in the README or giving `just clean` a sweep of that directory, because the error message points at the wrong file and will cost someone an afternoon.

## The invariant check is two levels, because one level was too expensive

`i2p_netdb:self_check/1` is O(n log n) and at the shipped capacity of 5000 routers it measures **315 us**. Run after every store that would have been a tax of roughly 315 us on a write path, to catch a bug the cheap check already catches.

So it is split:

- **`f:consistent/1`** -- O(1). `ets:info/2` size against `gb_trees:size/1` twice. This runs after **every** router mutation, and it is the check that catches the failure this arrangement actually risks: a promote that adds a position without dropping the old one, which shows up immediately as a count disagreement because `f:count/1` reads the order while the table holds one RouterInfo.
- **`f:self_check/1`** -- the full cross-check, for the operations that rewrite many entries at once: a **load** and the **expiry sweep**. Those are exactly where a partial bug is hardest to see, and exactly where a per-store O(1) check would not see it.

That is the same split the maintainer asked for on the recency order: keep the thing that needs concurrent read in ETS, keep everything else a value, and put the checking in the one place that can see both.

## Solution

Committed `qrrurtnm`. The per-frame existence check is a table read.

### Measured, final tree

742 ns for a `gen_server` round trip that does nothing at all, so the "before" figures have a floor to be read against:

| per-frame existence check | before | after | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| round trip that does nothing | 742 ns | — | reference |
| next hop unknown | 1364 ns | **78 ns** | 17.5x |
| next hop held | 2106 ns | **85 ns** | 24.8x |

Both a miss and a hit, because they are not the same operation, and the difference between them *is* the ticket: on a hit `find/1` additionally copies a RouterInfo out of the store, which is `2106 - 1364 = 742` ns of copying a value the caller had already thrown away.

The miss row settles what the cost was. `find/1` on a miss sat **622 ns above a call that does nothing** — so the lookup itself cost almost nothing and the cost was the mail. That matches the 1.39 us / 1.28 us floor ratio in the original description: there was no slow lookup to optimise, only a round trip to delete.

The held row is the steady state on a working transit hop, and it is where the win is largest.

### Criterion by criterion

1. **No round trip, no RouterInfo copied.** `ets:member/2`. The relay path also cannot block behind a NetDb write now, which the `gen_server:call` did.
2. **Unchanged behaviour when the next hop is unknown.** Still a silent drop; the peer manager still owns reconnection. What changed is that the drop is now *visible*.
3. **One authority for the existence question.** `ets:member` on one table cannot disagree with itself, and `f:has_router/1` is the only function that answers it.
4. **A test asserting no blocking call per frame.** `apps/i2per/test/i2p_tunnel_relay_tests.erl`, by trace rather than by assertion about the code. **Demonstrated red**: reverting `has_router/1` to `find/1` turns 3 of 4 cases red, green again on restore. Zero tolerance, not "fewer calls".
5. **The remaining lookup is counted.** New counter `transit_frames_dropped_no_route`.

### Both call sites, and the five left alone

`f:send_tunnel_data/2` (per frame, the hot one) and `f:forward_stb/4` (per build record).

The other five `f:find/1` callers in `src/` were each checked and deliberately left: `i2p_lookup_srv.erl:262` returns the RouterInfo, `i2p_peer.erl:927` reads its SSU2 address options, `i2p_peer.erl:1226` relays the whole RouterInfo back, `i2p_peer.erl:1475` connects to it, `i2p_tunnel_build.erl:393` needs its identity key. None is an existence check, so this is exactly as wide as the ticket.

add.issue.name: The peer manager's outbound queue is unbounded, and nothing ever drains it

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y

## What to build

An outbound queue that cannot grow without bound, and a stated policy for what happens to a frame that will never be sent.

`i2p_peer:send_when_ready/2` hands a message to the peer manager, which sends it if there is a live outbound conn or a live inbound session, and otherwise queues it in `pending_sends` via `f:enqueue_send/3`. That queue has **no depth cap and no age**. It is drained by exactly one path — `f:send_pending_sends/4`, called only when a connection to that peer actually succeeds (`i2p_peer.erl:470` and `:606`). Every other outcome leaves the entry in place forever.

`grep -n "maps:remove" apps/i2per/src/i2p_peer.erl` confirms it: the only removal from `pending_sends` is line 1746, inside `send_pending_sends/4`. There is no peer eviction and no `pending_sends` expiry anywhere — `peers` is never removed from either.

### The sharp case: queued, and nothing will ever be attempted

`f:maybe_connect/2` runs **after** the message is already queued, and it declines to dial in three ways:

- `network_allowed/2` returns false — returns without dialing
- `find_peer_config/2` returns `undefined` — **no dial is ever attempted**, so no amount of waiting drains the queue
- peer status is `backoff` and the backoff has not elapsed

The second is the one that runs forever. A peer whose RouterInfo is in the NetDb but which has no usable published address produces a permanent queue that only grows. That is precisely the steady state of a transit router whose tunnel peers have gone away — which is the role this ticket's work was aimed at.

Note this is the **complement** of #W46KMT8, not an overlap. `transit_frames_dropped_no_route` counts frames dropped because the NetDb does not hold the next hop. This counts frames the NetDb *does* hold, handed to a peer that never connects. An operator needs both: the first says "we cannot route this", the second says "we routed it and could not deliver it".

### Why it matters

The entry is per peer hash, so the cost multiplies by the number of unreachable peers, and it is paid in the peer manager's heap — the process every send path goes through. Each queued relay frame retains an I2NP message map holding a 1028-byte body, so roughly a kilobyte of heap apiece plus map overhead.

The inbound rate is bounded, which is what keeps this slow rather than instant: the transit token bucket defaults to `transit_bandwidth_kbps = 64`, charged one token per frame. But a *rate* limit is not a *depth* limit. Sustained traffic toward a peer that never connects accumulates at the admitted rate for as long as the condition holds. Hours of a busy transit hop is gigabytes.

It is also silent. Nothing logs it, nothing counts it, and no test covers it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pending_sends` has a stated bound, and it is enforced. A depth cap per peer hash is the obvious shape; if the answer is instead to refuse to queue at all beyond some depth, say so and count the refusal — a frame dropped for want of queue space is a different operator fact from one dropped for want of a route.
- [ ] Entries are **aged**, or at minimum removed when the peer is. Whatever the bound, decide and document what happens to a queued frame when the peer becomes unreachable permanently: is it sent later, expired, or dropped with a count? "Silently for ever" is not one of the options.
- [ ] The refusal/drop path is counted, so an operator can tell queue exhaustion apart from a routing failure. A new counter in `m:i2p_stats` following #W46KMT8's `transit_frames_dropped_no_route`; a counter, not an event, for the same reason — this is a steady state, not an incident.
- [ ] The bound is reachable in a test. A test that asserts the queue stays under the cap after N enqueues against a peer that never connects, rather than a test that reads the cap back.
- [ ] Decided in the same place: **`peers` has no cap either.** No eviction, no expiry — `peers => #{}` at init and nothing ever removes from it. That is either the same ticket or a distinct one; it should not be discovered later by whoever profiles this.

## Notes for whoever picks this up

Found while measuring the relay path for #W46KMT8, and verified in the code rather than inferred: the four call sites above, the single removal, and the three `maybe_connect` decline paths were each read. The bound itself is a design call — a per-peer depth cap, an age, or refusing to queue at all are all defensible, and the acceptance criteria are written so that any of them satisfies it as long as the behaviour is stated and observable.

add.issue.name: i2p_netdb mutates its ETS table in place while documenting itself as a value

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y
Found while scoping #PPW41Y4.

## What is wrong

**`i2p_netdb:store/0` mutates the ETS table in place, but the module still documents itself as pure.** Since #W46KMT8 the store is `#{routers => ets:tid(), order => gb_tree, order_pos => gb_tree, ...}`, and every mutator writes to that table directly:

- `f:store/3` -> `f:insert_newer/5` -> `ets:insert`
- `f:remove/2` -> `ets:delete`
- `f:remove_expired/3` -> `f:partition_routers/3` -> `ets:delete`
- `f:trim/1` -> `ets:delete`

The returned store therefore carries **only the recency trees**. The RouterInfos are already gone into the table whether or not the caller keeps the result, so a caller that drops the return value -- which the previous contract explicitly invited -- leaves a store whose two halves disagree.

## Demonstrated

```
{_S1b, added} = i2p_netdb:store(S1, RI2, Now),   %% return value dropped

S1 : table=2  count/1=1  consistent={error,{size_disagreement,
                              #{table => 2, order => 1, order_pos => 1}}}
      to_binary/1       -> 706 bytes    %% RI2 never reaches the file
      routers/1         -> 1 entry      %% the table holds 2
      remove_expired/3  -> 0 removed
```

The failure is silent and lossy: a router the table holds is invisible to every listing, is never persisted, and is never expired. `f:count/1` reads the order, not the table, so the count is wrong too.

`f:consistent/1` catches it -- that is precisely the failure the O(1) check was built for -- but only when somebody calls it, and `i2p_netdb` is a public module. Its own moduledoc and `-type store()` both still promise immutability:

> The store is a value the gen_server in `m:i2p_netdb_srv` owns, and every operation returns a new one.

## Why this is more than a docstring

Nothing in the tree currently drops a return value -- `f:remove_expired/3` and `f:store/3` are only called by the gen_server, which keeps its result -- so this is a trap rather than a live bug. It matters for two reasons:

1. **It is a trap with no rail.** The module's stated contract is the opposite of its behaviour, and the failure is silent data loss. That is the kind of thing a future caller gets wrong.
2. **It blocks #PPW41Y4.** That ticket has to hand the store, or a copy of it, to a writer process that serialises and fsyncs and to a sweeper that walks the recency order. If the table mutates under whoever holds the store, handing it over hands over a handle to live shared state and the two processes race with no way to detect it. #PPW41Y4 needs an honest answer here first.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The contract matches the behaviour: either the store becomes a real value again, or the mutators are named and documented as in-place and the type says so.
- [ ] If the store keeps its table, there is one function through which the table is reached, and the module's central property ("one function stands between every mutation and both structures") is true of the code rather than only of the docstring.
- [ ] A test that drops the return value of a mutator and asserts the store is **not** silently corrupt -- either because it is a value and nothing happens, or because the corruption is loud.
- [ ] `f:to_binary/1`, `f:routers/1`, `f:keys/1`, `f:count/1` and `f:remove_expired/3` all agree with the table about what the store holds, in the test above and in the normal case.
- [ ] Decide, and record, whether `f:has_router/2` -- which reads the table directly and is now the hot read -- can be given a snapshot instead. That is the option that unblocks #PPW41Y4 cleanly, and it is a design fork, so it is the maintainer's call.

add.issue.comment.md:
## Scoped and measured. One defect found, filed as #QDA7A0X, and it gates part of this ticket.

Measured on this machine (OTP 28.5), store at the shipped capacity of 5000.

| work | measured | runs in the read process today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `f:router_info:decode/1` (Ed25519 verify) | **100.4 us** | yes, per RouterInfo stored |
| `f:netdb:to_binary/1`, 5000 routers | **15 856 us** | yes, every 15 min |
| file write + fsync + rename of that 3.4 MB | **924 us** | yes |
| `f:netdb:remove_expired/3`, 5000 live | **12 942 us** | yes, every 30 min |
| `f:netdb:store/3`, new key, at capacity | 3.1 us | yes |

So a **save stalls reads for ~16.8 ms** and a **sweep for ~12.9 ms**. Those two are the real cost; the per-store path is already cheap. The description's 90.01 us for a verify is right, I get 100.4 us.

Two numbers that contradict what is on the board:

- **`f:self_check/1` is 5370 us at capacity 5000, not the 315 us in #W46KMT8's Solution** -- that figure came from a smaller store. The O(1) `f:consistent/1` split is still right and does not reopen, but the load and the expiry sweep each pay 5.4 ms for the full check, and both are on the list of things to move.
- **Copying the whole store to another process is 541 us**, measured as a real send (155 030 words). So handing the store to a writer costs 541 us and saves 15 856 us. The copy does not have to be free; it has to be 30x cheaper than the work.

## The defect, and why it gates the second half

Since #W46KMT8 the store owns an ETS table and `f:store/3`, `f:remove/2`, `f:remove_expired/3` and `f:trim/1` write to it **in place**. The returned store carries only the recency trees, so a caller that drops it -- which the module's own docstring invites -- silently loses routers: `f:count/1` under-reports, `f:to_binary/1` omits them, `f:routers/1` hides them. Demonstrated and filed as **#QDA7A0X**.

That gates the two sweeps here, because moving them off the read path means handing the store to a writer and a sweeper. While the table mutates under whoever holds it, that is handing over a handle to live shared state. Fixing it is a design fork (real value again, or a published read-only view), so it is the maintainer's call, not mine.

## Starting with the piece that does not depend on the fork

**Signature verification off the read path.** It needs no shared store: a signature is verified from bytes, and the caller ends up with a value either way. `f:store_binary/2` is currently a call carrying raw bytes, with the 100 us decode inside the NetDb process. Decode outside it and send the parsed RouterInfo, and a floodfill burst or a 75-RouterInfo reseed bundle costs the NetDb 75 x 3.1 us instead of 75 x 103 us.

The ticket's test -- a burst of stores, then assert a read is still served -- is a **barrier**, not a deadline: issue the burst, then read, assert the answer. Whether it was red before is checked by reverting the change and watching it fail, as #W46KMT8 did.

Not yet run: dialyzer, CT, full gate. Not yet decided: both sweeps, pending #QDA7A0X.

add.issue.comment.md:
## Measured before designing: a verifier pool cannot work on this OTP, so the design changed

I had planned `m:i2p_netdb_verify` as a small pool of verifier processes, so two stores could verify at once instead of queueing. **I measured it before building it, and the measurement says no.** A pool would have added a supervisor child, a module and a registered name to buy nothing.

### The result

Same harness for every row: split 96 items into 1 or 8 processes, one process per chunk, count the items each one completed, best of 5. The count is checked, so a dropped chunk is a loud failure and not a suspiciously good speedup. (Two earlier harnesses of mine dropped work through bad index arithmetic and reported 8x speedups that did not exist. This one peels chunks off the front and counts.)

| workload | 1 process | 8 processes | ratio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| raw `crypto:verify/5` (the NIF) | 31.0/ms | 18.1/ms | **0.58x** |
| `m:i2p_crypto:ed25519_verify/3` | 30.6/ms | 16.3/ms | **0.53x** |
| `m:i2p_router_info:parse/1` | 35.9/ms | 17.7/ms | **0.49x** |
| `m:i2p_router_info:decode/1` | 37.4/ms | 16.7/ms | **0.45x** |
| `phash2`, no crypto (control) | 685.7/ms | 2909.1/ms | **4.24x** |

**Ed25519 verification does not get faster with more processes here, and total throughput gets worse.** The control is what makes that believable: same spawn/receive structure, same slices, crypto the only difference, and it scales 4.24x. Sixteen schedulers online, load average 1.16, so the box was not the constraint.

I have not established *why* -- whether it is a lock inside the crypto NIF or an OpenSSL build detail. It does not change the decision, and finding out is a separate piece of work.

### What this rules out, and what it leaves

Ruled out: a pool of verifier processes. N processes would queue behind the same serialising thing one process does, and pay N copies of the hand-off.

Still true, and still the win: **one verification is 100.4 us and the store is 1-3 us.** Whether it runs in a pool or in the caller, it must not run in `m:i2p_netdb_srv`, which is the process every NetDb read queues behind.

So the change is the simple one. `f:store_binary/2` and `f:store_ls_binary/2` decode in the **calling** process and hand the NetDb a parsed RouterInfo or LeaseSet. No new process, no supervisor child, nothing to supervise.

The cost of that choice, stated plainly: the peer manager and the transit relay each pay 100 us per store they receive, where before the NetDb paid it. That is a relocation, not a removal, and it is the right one only because the NetDb is the process everything else waits on. `#VXRH456` (crypto off the normal schedulers) is the ticket that attacks the 100 us itself rather than where it runs.

add.issue.comment.md:
## Blocking PPW41Y4, and here is the decision that unblocks it

`#PPW41Y4` has to move two things off the process that serves NetDb reads: the 15-minute disk save and the 30-minute expiry sweep. Both mean handing the store to another process, and that is not safe while the store mutates in place.

So the question this ticket exists to answer is narrow and concrete: **can the store be handed to another process, and if so what does the receiving process get?**

### What the measurements say is available

Recorded on #PPW41Y4 so the decision is priced:

- serialising 5000 routers to bytes: **15 856 us**
- copying the whole store between processes: **541 us** (155 030 words)
- the file write and fsync of the result: **924 us**
- an expiry sweep at 5000 routers: **12 942 us**

So the copy is about **30x cheaper than the work**, which means the decision does not have to make the store free to copy. It only has to make handing it over mean something.

### The three answers I can see

**(a) A snapshot, explicitly.** A function that returns a value the writer can serialise without touching live state. The recency order is already a value in the store map, and the RouterInfos are in the table, so a snapshot is "the order plus a consistent read of the table". The hard part is the consistency: the table can change under the reader, so the snapshot has to either tolerate that or the writer has to be the only thing that can write. Tolerating it is fine for a periodic save, since a router evicted mid-save is one that was leaving anyway.

**(b) Publish a read-only view, as `?ROUTER_TABLE` already does for `f:has_router/2`.** The writer gets the tid and reads it directly, and the save is by definition a moment-old snapshot. This is the smallest change and it matches a pattern the codebase has already accepted. What it costs is that the write path is now reachable from two places, which is the property the module's docstring currently claims and does not have.

**(c) Put the table back to being a value and give the read path its own published view.** The honest fix, and the most work. It makes every existing guarantee in the module true again, at the cost of undoing the part of #W46KMT8 that made the per-frame read a table read.

### What I would pick, and why it is not my call

(b) is the cheapest thing that works and it reuses an existing decision. (a) is the one that keeps a single writer, which is the property most worth keeping, at the price of a snapshot function that has to be correct about concurrent eviction. (c) is the only one that makes the module's stated contract true.

I have not implemented any of them. This is a design fork with blast radius past its own ticket, it changes a contract other code and comments already rely on, and the maintainer settled the ETS arrangement two commits ago with a written rationale. Re-drawing that inside a performance ticket is not my decision to make.

Recorded so the next session does not re-derive it: the measurements, the three options, and the reason the ticket is parked.

add.issue.comment.md:
## The dropped-return-value bug is worse than this ticket describes, and the check meant to catch it does not

Investigating before designing, because the acceptance criteria lean on `f:consistent/1` catching this. It does not, and the case it misses is the common one.

The ticket's demonstration is the easy case: dropping the return value of an **insert** makes the counts disagree, and `f:consistent/1` says `{size_disagreement, ...}`.

### Dropping the return value of a promote is invisible

A promote replaces one key's `Seq` in place. The table keeps the same rows, the order keeps the same entries, `order_pos` is still the exact inverse of `order`, and no two entries share a `Seq`. Every invariant `f:self_check/1` knows how to check still holds.

Three routers inserted A, B, C so A is least-recent. Re-store A with a newer timestamp, drop the return value:

```
before the promote    MRU-first = CBA
after, correct store  MRU-first = ACB

against the STALE store:
  consistent/1 : ok
  self_check/1  : ok
  count/1 = 3, table size = 3        (they agree)
  keys/1     = CBA                   <- the pre-promote order, permanently
  order_pos for A = 1                <- truth is 4
```

**It does not self-heal.** An unrelated store afterwards leaves the order reading `CBA` and `consistent/1` reading `ok`. The store is not momentarily wrong, it is wrong from then on.

### What it costs, both measured

**The router that was just re-stored is the next one evicted.** Capacity 2 holding A and B; promote A; insert C:

| | holds after inserting C |
| --- | --- |
| return value kept | C, A (B evicted, correct) |
| return value dropped | C, B (**A** evicted) |

`f:trim/1` evicts the smallest `Seq`, and the stale order still has A at `Seq` 1. The freshest RouterInfo is the first one thrown away, at capacity, and `consistent/1` reports `ok` on the result.

**The wrong order is written to disk and inherited on reload**, because `f:to_binary/1` walks the order tree:

```
order before save         CBA
order after save + reload CB
f:self_check/1 on the reloaded store: ok
```

### Why this changes the shape of the fix

The third criterion asks for a test that drops a return value and asserts the store is not silently corrupt. Size-based checks cannot satisfy that: they detect a row that appeared or vanished, and are blind to a row whose position changed, which is exactly what a promote produces. Any fix leaning on `f:consistent/1` leans on a check that provably misses the interesting failure.

The second comment lists the three ways out. None is a small change and two of them re-draw a decision the maintainer settled with a written rationale, so I have implemented none of them yet. No code changed this session.

edit.description.md:
Part of #CBNYQ9Y
Found while scoping #PPW41Y4. **Updated 2026-10-01: the bug is worse than first filed, and the fix is a design fork. See "What changed on investigation".**

## What is wrong

**`i2p_netdb:store/0` mutates the ETS table in place, but the module still documents itself as pure.** Since #W46KMT8 the store is `#{routers => ets:tid(), order => gb_tree, order_pos => gb_tree, ...}`, and every mutator writes to that table directly:

- `f:store/3` -> `f:insert_newer/5` -> `ets:insert`
- `f:remove/2` -> `ets:delete`
- `f:remove_expired/3` -> `f:partition_routers/3` -> `ets:delete`
- `f:trim/1` -> `ets:delete`

The returned store carries **only the recency trees**. The RouterInfos are already in the table whether or not the caller keeps the result, so a caller that drops the return value leaves a store whose two halves disagree.

## Demonstrated

Dropping the return value of an **insert**:

```
{_S1b, added} = i2p_netdb:store(S1, RI2, Now),   %% return value dropped

S1 : table=2  count/1=1  consistent={error,{size_disagreement,
                              #{table => 2, order => 1, order_pos => 1}}}
      to_binary/1       -> 706 bytes    %% RI2 never reaches the file
      routers/1         -> 1 entry      %% the table holds 2
      remove_expired/3  -> 0 removed
```

The failure is silent and lossy: a router the table holds is invisible to every listing, is never persisted, and is never expired.

## What changed on investigation

**`f:consistent/1` does not catch this in the case that matters, and neither does `f:self_check/1`.** Both tickets were leaning on that check. A promote replaces one key's `Seq` in place, so the table and the order keep the same number of entries, `order_pos` stays the exact inverse of `order`, and no two `Seq`s collide. Every invariant the checks know about still holds.

Three routers inserted A, B, C so A is least-recent; re-store A with a newer timestamp and drop the return value:

```
before the promote    MRU-first = CBA
after, correct store  MRU-first = ACB

stale store:  consistent/1 = ok   self_check/1 = ok
              count/1 = 3 = table size    keys/1 = CBA (wrong, permanently)
```

It does not self-heal either. An unrelated store leaves the order wrong and the check green.

### Two measured consequences

**The freshest RouterInfo is the first one evicted.** Capacity 2 holding A and B; promote A; insert C. Keeping the return value leaves C, A. Dropping it leaves C, **B** -- A, the router just re-stored, is evicted, because `f:trim/1` takes the smallest `Seq` and the stale order still has A at `Seq` 1. `consistent/1` reports `ok` on that store.

**The wrong order is persisted and inherited.** `f:to_binary/1` walks the order tree, so a save writes the pre-promote sequence and `f:from_binary/1` restores it. The reloaded store passes `f:self_check/1`.

So the third acceptance criterion below cannot be met by a better size check. The checks detect a row that appeared or vanished and are blind to a row whose position changed.

## The decision this needs

Three ways out, none of them small, two of them re-drawing a decision the maintainer settled with a written rationale:

- **A version counter in the table.** A generation bumped on every mutation, compared by the store, so staleness is detectable in O(1) by a check that cannot miss. Cheap, and a *detector* rather than a fix: the store is still a handle to live state.
- **Put the recency order in the table as well.** One structure, nothing to drift, the whole bug class goes rather than being detected. This makes the module's stated contract true, and it is the option #W46KMT8's rationale argued against (a second table is side-effect state, and the "one function between every mutation and both structures" property is about the code, not just the docstring).
- **Make the table a value again** and give the hot read its own published view. Largest change, and it reverts the per-frame read to a table read.

There is a fourth that the investigation makes worth considering, because the promote case is the one that hurts: **derive the order from the table** rather than storing it. If each row carried its own `Seq`, the order is a sort of the rows and there is no second structure to fall behind. The cost is that finding the LRU becomes a scan rather than a `gb_trees:take_smallest/1`, which matters at capacity 5000. That trade has not been measured.

## Why this is more than a docstring

Nothing in the tree currently drops a return value, so this is a trap rather than a live bug. It matters because:

1. **It is a trap with no rail.** The stated contract is the opposite of the behaviour, and the failure is silent data loss that no existing check sees.
2. **It blocks #PPW41Y4.** That ticket must hand the store to a writer that serialises and fsyncs and to a sweeper that walks the recency order. While the table mutates in place, handing it over hands over a handle to live shared state and the two processes race undetectably.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The contract matches the behaviour: either the store becomes a real value again, or the mutators are named and documented as in-place and the type says so.
- [ ] If the store keeps its table, there is one function through which the table is reached, and the module's central property is true of the code rather than only of the docstring.
- [ ] A test that drops the return value of a **promote** (not just an insert) and asserts the store is not silently corrupt. A size check cannot satisfy this; see above.
- [ ] A test that drops the return value of a mutate-at-capacity operation and asserts the router just re-stored is not the eviction victim.
- [ ] `f:to_binary/1`, `f:routers/1`, `f:keys/1`, `f:count/1` and `f:remove_expired/3` agree with the table about what the store holds, in the normal case and after a dropped return value.
- [ ] The design fork above is decided and recorded, with the measurement behind whichever option is taken.

add.issue.comment.md:
## The fourth option, priced: deriving the order from the table is 500x more expensive per insert

I flagged "put the Seq in the table row and derive the order" as worth considering but unmeasured. Here it is, at the shipped capacity of 5000, so the fork can be decided on numbers rather than on taste.

| operation | measured | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gb_trees:take_smallest/1`, **today's LRU lookup** | **0.9 us** | O(log n) |
| `ets:select` min over the table | 478.6 us | the cheapest full scan |
| `ets:foldl` min over the table | 2286.2 us | |
| `ets:tab2list` + `lists:min/1` | 7129.2 us | copies every row |
| `ets:select` + `keysort`, the derived order | 8337.4 us | |
| `ets:tab2list` + `sort`, the derived order | 11957.5 us | |
| `f:store/3` at capacity, for scale | 124.7 us | |
| `f:to_binary/1`, the 15-minute save, for scale | 7416.8 us | |

**Deriving the LRU victim costs 478 us against 0.9 us today, a 530x regression on the eviction path.** And that is the best case: `ets:select` still walks all 5000 rows and builds a list of 5000 keys to find a minimum. It would be paid on every insert into a full store, which is exactly when the router is busiest.

I can see the argument for it anyway, and it is not a bad one: the order would stop being a second structure, so the promote bug could not exist at all, which is stronger than detecting it. But 478 us per insert is a real price and it is on the write path of a router that is trying to get off the read path. **My recommendation is against this option**, and I would not build it without the maintainer overriding that.

Note also that the derived *order* (8.3-12.0 ms) is cheaper than the 15-minute save (7.4 ms) only in the sense that both are periodic. `f:keys/1` and `f:routers/1` call the order on every invocation, and `f:to_binary/1` is the save, so a derived order would make the save itself sort 5000 rows on top of serialising them.

### So the fork narrows to three, and the cost table now reads

- **Version counter in the table** -- O(1) check, no change to the store path, makes staleness *detectable* rather than impossible. Cheapest, and it is a detector.
- **Recency order in the table as a second structure** -- one atomic unit, no drift, contract becomes true, single-writer enforced by `protected` as it already is. The cost is giving up the `gb_trees` order, so eviction becomes a scan at 478 us, unless a second table can answer "smallest Seq" in O(1) some other way, which I have not found.
- **Table back to a value, hot read gets its own published view** -- the contract is true by construction, and it reverts the per-frame read to something the read path no longer shares with writes.

All three are now priced enough to choose between. It remains a maintainer's call: two of them re-draw a decision settled with a written rationale in #W46KMT8, and that is not mine to reverse inside a bug ticket.

add.issue.name: HUMAN INPUT: how should the NetDb store's two structures be reconciled?

edit.description.md:
HUMAN INPUT: which way should the NetDb store be fixed? #QDA7A0X is blocked on this.

Part of #CBNYQ9Y
Blocks #QDA7A0X, which in turn blocks the two sweeps in #PPW41Y4.

## The decision

`i2p_netdb` has two structures that must agree: an ETS table of RouterInfos and a `gb_trees` pair holding the recency order. The table is mutated in place, so the store is a handle to live state while the module documents it as a value. A caller that drops a mutator's return value gets silent, permanent data loss, and **neither `f:consistent/1` nor `f:self_check/1` sees the promote case.**

Full evidence and measurements on #QDA7A0X. What is needed is a choice between these.

## Option 1: a version counter in the table

A generation number bumped on every mutation, held in the table and compared by the store, so a stale store is detectable in O(1) by a check that cannot miss.

- **For:** cheapest by a wide margin. No change to the store path (`f:store/3` is 124.7 us at capacity and stays there). Nothing about the read path changes. The check is exact rather than heuristic, which is what the promote case needs.
- **Against:** it is a **detector, not a fix.** The store is still a handle to live state, so a caller that ignores the error still has a corrupt store, and it is corrupt in a new way: it now knows it is corrupt. It also does not unblock #PPW41Y4, because handing the store to a writer process is still handing over live state. It would need the check to be enforced rather than advisory, which means every mutator raises on a stale store, which turns a silent bug into a crash and is a behaviour change.

## Option 2: the recency order becomes a second table

One atomic structure, so there is nothing to drift and the module's stated contract becomes true. Single-writer is already enforced by `protected`.

- **For:** removes the bug class rather than detecting it. Two structures written by one function, so "one function stands between every mutation and both structures" becomes true of the code.
- **Against:** the `gb_trees` order exists to make eviction O(log n) at **0.9 us**. Finding the LRU victim across 5000 table rows costs **478.6 us** with the cheapest scan, a 530x regression on the write path. `f:store/3` is 124.7 us today, so eviction would dominate it. A full derived order is 8.3-12.0 ms, which would also be paid inside the 7.4 ms save.
- **This is the one that re-draws a settled decision.** #W46KMT8's rationale says a second table is side-effect state and the module's central property is about the code rather than the docstring. That reasoning is still sound; what has changed is that the property is now load-bearing for a bug nobody had found yet.

## Option 3: the table becomes a value again

Revert to a map, and give the per-frame existence check its own published read-only view, the way `?ROUTER_TABLE` already works.

- **For:** the contract is true by construction, so the whole class of bug is gone rather than detected. Keeps the 0.9 us eviction and the 0.2 us `f:has_router/2` read.
- **Against:** largest change, and it reverts the part of #W46KMT8 that made the per-frame read cheap. Every mutator copies the map, so `f:store/3` at capacity 5000 goes from O(log n) to O(n). A published read view is a second structure again, so the problem does not vanish, it moves to the boundary between the store and the view.

## What I would pick, and why it is not my call

**Option 1 with the check enforced**, if the priority is a small safe change now: it is the only one that is cheap, and it converts silent corruption into a loud failure, which is what the ticket's third criterion actually asks for ("not silently corrupt -- either because it is a value and nothing happens, or because the corruption is loud").

**Option 3** if the priority is that #PPW41Y4 can actually be finished, because it is the only one where handing the store to another process means something.

I have not implemented any of them. Two of the three re-draw a decision the maintainer settled two commits ago with a written rationale, and the choice changes what a public module promises. That is a maintainer's call.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One option is chosen and recorded here, with the reasoning.
- [ ] The two rejected options say why, so the next reader does not re-derive them.
- [ ] #QDA7A0X and #PPW41Y4 are unblocked.
